title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Summary:
If you want a mid-range machine that's future proof for at least the next few years, this fits the bill nicely. Get a chip that trades blows with an i9-9900K for $200 less and uses less power doing it. Yes, Intel's higher clock speed will allow it to be faster at certain workloads & games, but it's usually not by much. Regarding gaming, if you're running at 1080p or 1440p and not running a top of the line video card, the difference between the 3700x and 9900K is negligible. For workstation use, it's a no brainer, unless you want to up to a 3900x.

Building computers and keeping up to date with all the latest hardware is my hobby and second job. I was an AMD guy back in the Athlon XP & Athlon 64 days, but once it was Sandy Bridge vs Buldozer, there was basically no reason to go AMD. For years, I built basically nothing but Intel Machines. Ryzen's intro was exciting to me, AMD is now competitive again! But other than a couple of builds for people, I skipped the first 2 generations. Now, Gen 2 chips are cheap, and Gen 3 chips can not only hold there own, but often outperform Intel in many tasks, sometimes even gaming! And even when they loose, it's not by much.

So the 3700x gives great performance for the money, but what about stability and easy of setup? Well, it's nearly as good as Intel. Regarding stability, I'd say their fantastic as long as you avoid AMD Video Card drivers, which are a bit flaky at the moment. But with an Nvidia card, rock stable. Now, I said nearly as good as intel due to the drivers, BIOS updates, and power and voltage situation. For most current intel systems, the platform is so mature that everything generally just works out of the box. No drivers or power plans required, Windows 10 knows what to do with the platform. But with AMD Zen 2, there are potential issues on older chip-sets and not being able to boot without BIOS updates, performance issues with older BIOS updates, etc. On top of that, you really want to get the chip-set drivers & power plans to have the best configuration. None of this is hard, but Intel is already so integrated into Windows 10. But with Ryzen gaining market-share at their current pace, integration and optimization will be there soon.

Most of the time, you want to build a balanced system. Here are my CPU suggestions based on price points (Approximations)

$500 to $800 builds: 1600X AF (Which is basically a 2600X)
$800 to $1300 Builds: 3600
$1200 to $2500 Builds: 3700X
$1800 to $3400 Builds: 3900X
$2500+ Builds: $3950X

My wife and I rebuild our gaming systems this past Holiday season. Here's my latest rig with this chip:
Processor: AMD 3700X
Video Card: Nvidia GTX 1070 (used)
RAM: 32GB G-Skill Dual Channel 3600Mhz CAS16
Motherboard: MSI X570 Carbon (Good For 3800X and below, VRMs may run hot on 3900X and above)
Sound: Sound Blaster Z
SSD: 1GB A-DATA SX8200 Pro & 2x 2TB Crucial (1100 & MX500)
PSU: Seasonic 750W Gold
Case: Fractal Design Define C
CPU Cooler: Noctua DH-15
Fans: 4x 140mm Noctua AF-14 & 1x 120mm Noctua AF-12

Gaming and productivity have been fantastic with no issues. I really want more GPU power, but I'm waiting for the prices to come down for Nvidia or for AMD to get their driver act together. GTX 1070s can be had for under $200 used, and compare well to GTX 1660 Supers (We got ours before this was an option). If you have the money The 2070 S would be my go to. I could have invested the cost of the expensive fans and CPU cooler to a faster video card or 3900x, but having a system that's quiet, cool, and fast is important to me.

Here's to hoping Ryzen continues down this path!

En si ha dado un buen paso en comparación al 2700x que es el que tenía anteriormente, de media sobre 10/20 fps a los juegos que normalmente juego, no entrare a valorar con otros juegos que nunca he usado, en multitarea la verdad que también he notado algo de mejoría respecto al 2700x.

En cuanto a compatibilidad con la memoria, de momento no he tenido ningún problema en ponerlas a 3600, también decir que justo me ha llegado cuando han sacado el micro código AGESA 1.0.0.3AB para Asus, pero también me he encontrado con algún, pero, que ahora los comentare.

Hacer OC ahora mismo con las bios que hay es bastante absurdo, saca bastante mas rendimiento en modo auto y con el PBO, pero también tiene algunas cosas que no me han gustado, por ejemplo el Voltaje se dispara, AMD ya ha salido diciendo que es normal, pero para mi gusto demasiado alto, tiene picos que casi llegan a 1.5v, luego las temperaturas dentro de Windows si no se activa el modo Balanceo de RYZEN son bastante altas, estamos hablando de una media de 50º y eso que voy con liquida custom, con la actualización del chipset y el modo balanceo la cosa ya cambia, esta en idle sobre 38º, en full carga alcanza sobre los 70º también por el alto voltaje que hay, espero que en poco tiempo mejoren este aspecto como en las anteriores generaciones.

En cuanto si vale la pena coger la plataforma X570, en mi opinión por el precio que tiene si no es que necesitas el PCIE 4.0 mas vale coger una B450 o X470 y el dinero que sobra invertirlo en otro apartado.

El apartado que menos me ha gustado, también hay que decir que depende del fabricante ahora mismo, es en el apartado de BIOS, apenas puedes tocar muchas cosas, dado que a la mínima ya no arranca, lo mejor a día de hoy estando como están la BIOS que se tienen que pulir es dejarlo en modo AUTO el apartado del procesado.

Resumiendo, me parece una gran procesador y AMD ha vuelto hacer un producto muy competitivo, pero con precios ajustados, aun no hace ni un mes que han salido y bueno creo que las bios las tienen que pulir aun bastante, espero que para setiembre ya estén bien pulidas y poder aun exprimir mas el potencial de este procesador, a medida que vayan mejorando iré subiendo que tal va la mejora.

EDITO:
Justo ayer sacaron nueva BIOS y nuevo código de chipset, ahora ya he podido tocar parte del overclock, decir que en el tema voltajes aun me hace extraños o no mide muy bien la temperatura pero con el tema de OC en BIOS ahora va perfecto, he conseguido poner en nada las rams a 3600 con cl 16-16-15-15-32-42 y uns subtimings bastante bajos, el procesador lo he subido hasta 4.3Mhz con un voltaje de 1.280v no obstante las temperaturas me siguen exactamente igual, solo bajan las temperaturas a rangos normales cuando el procesador lo dejo en stock y si PBO ni nada, el stock del mismo son 3600Mhz todo lo que pase de allí las temperaturas se disparan, supongo que tienen que pulir aun mas los microcódigos y las bios, pero de momento van bien encaminados, cuando pongan otro cambio volveré a editar.

For the price, the performance is amazing, there's a reason it's one of the best CPUs on the market to this day. For those who are curious about gaming I'm using a 3060 ti with this CPU at 1440P (and previously at 4K) so the 12100F was hitting about 100 percent when the GPU was but now the 14700 sits at 5 to 25 percent during gaming. If you have a 3060 ti then use a 12100F there's no reason to use a 14700, I needed this one for piano VSTs to run and for Distant Horizons chunk loading specifically.

Overall Rating: 4.5 out of 5 stars

For: Serious gamers, demanding content creators, overclocking enthusiasts, those upgrading from older systems

Against: Pricey compared to previous generations, runs hot, requires beefy cooling

Performance: 5 out of 5 stars

The i7-13700K packs a serious punch. Its hybrid architecture with 8 performance cores and 8 efficient cores tackles demanding tasks with ease. Whether you're pushing pixels in the latest AAA titles or crunching numbers in complex spreadsheets, this CPU thrives under pressure. In gaming, expect silky-smooth frames at 1440p and beyond, even in the most demanding titles. Compared to its predecessor, the i7-12700K, it offers a noticeable performance boost, especially in multi-threaded workloads.

Overclocking: 4.5 out of 5 stars

The i7-13700K is an overclocker's dream. It offers plenty of headroom for pushing clock speeds, unlocking even more performance potential. However, remember that this comes at the cost of increased power consumption and heat generation. Ensure you have a robust cooling solution like a high-end air cooler or AIO liquid cooler to keep things under control.

The i7-13700K boasts impressive specs: PCIe 5.0 support for next-gen hardware, DDR5 memory compatibility, and Intel UHD Graphics 770 for basic graphics needs. This future-proofs your build and ensures you're ready for the latest tech as it emerges. However, keep in mind that the cost of DDR5 memory might still be a drawback for some.

Value: 4 out of 5 stars

However, it still offers compelling value compared to its closest competitor, the AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, especially for gaming. Remember, you'll need to factor in the cost of a capable cooler and potentially DDR5 memory, further impacting the overall value proposition.

Things to Consider:

Heat and Power Consumption: This CPU runs hot, especially under overclocking. Invest in a robust cooling solution to avoid thermal throttling.
Price: The i7-13700K is expensive compared to older generations and slightly pricier than its main competitor. Consider your budget carefully.
DDR5 Compatibility: While future-proof, DDR5 memory is still more expensive than DDR4. Factor this into your overall build cost.
Final Verdict:

The Intel Core i7-13700K is a top-tier processor for serious gamers, demanding content creators, and overclocking enthusiasts. Its blistering performance, PCIe 5.0 and DDR5 support, and overclocking headroom make it a future-proof powerhouse. However, the high price, heat generation, and DDR5 compatibility requirements might be dealbreakers for some. If you're looking for the ultimate in gaming and multi-core performance and have the budget for a premium build, the i7-13700K is a worthy investment. Just be prepared to feed it some serious watts and keep it cool.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
These 13th and 14th gen chips are simultaneously horrible and great at the same time. They are horrible because of the well known Vmin shift causing degradation. Which (hopefully) has been addressed with microcode 0x12B. We will really only know in the next coming year if that’s the case.

Even with all the reasons not to buy Intel, I still invested in a dead platform with a possibly defective design. Why? These are probably the last monolithic desktop chips to ever be made. There is just no replacement for low latency, instant response computing. These will be slower in games and some production tasks, but will still feel faster than anything else on the market for day to day use, by a decent margin. And they will continue to feel superior, for a long, long time.

As for my chip, out of the box it wants to hit the CPU with 1.41v when stress testing. Even though that should be fine, even for 24/7 extended use, I still manually changed the IA VR Voltage limit to 1.38v. That brought the temps down by an incredible 20c, making it never break 70c.

Setting an IA VR voltage limit is not undervolting, it’s merely telling your motherboard to never go over said limit. So you will likely see a slight decrease in performance for the trade off of having less heat and stress on the CPU. It’s a very easy way for people less familiar with undervolting to make sure their CPU doesn’t fry itself.

The memory controller on my CPU is outstanding as well, and I haven’t had an issue running 2x16GB 7600mhz sticks. Just make sure your motherboard is the latest Z790 with an 8 layer PCB if you’re looking to take advantage of Intel’s superior memory support.

I’ve very happy with this CPU. I was disappointed to hear Intel will follow AMD down the road of high latency, sluggish chiplet/tile designs in the future. So if you like the feeling of a very snappy, lighting fast PC. These chips might be your last hope.

text:
L'Intel Core i7-13700K è uno dei processori desktop più potenti sul mercato, pensato per chi non vuole compromessi. Appartenente alla 13ª generazione (Raptor Lake), è la scelta prediletta per i gamer hardcore e i professionisti della creazione di contenuti.

Punti di Forza (Pro)

Architettura Ibrida (16 Core): La vera rivoluzione è l'architettura che combina potenza ed efficienza. Dispone di ben 16 core totali, suddivisi in 8 P-core (Performance) per i compiti pesanti e 8 E-core (Efficiency) per gestire i processi in background. Questa combinazione garantisce fluidità totale anche durante il multitasking pesante.

Velocità Turbo (5.4 GHz): Le frequenze sono altissime. Grazie alla tecnologia Intel Turbo Boost Max 3.0, può raggiungere una velocità di clock fino a 5,4 GHz. Questo si traduce in frame rate elevatissimi nei giochi e tempi di rendering ridotti.

Sbloccato per Overclock ("K"): Il suffisso "K" e la dicitura "UNLOCKED" sulla scatola indicano che il moltiplicatore è sbloccato. Gli utenti esperti possono spingerlo oltre i limiti di fabbrica per ottenere ancora più prestazioni (a patto di avere un raffreddamento adeguato).

Versatilità di Memoria e PCIe: È progettato per il futuro ma compatibile con il presente: supporta sia le nuove memorie DDR5 che le classiche DDR4, e offre linee PCIe 5.0 e 4.0 per le schede video e gli SSD più veloci in commercio.

Cache Generosa: Con 30 MB di Cache, il processore può accedere rapidamente a grandi quantità di dati, riducendo la latenza nei giochi e nelle applicazioni complesse.

Aspetti da Considerare (Contro)

Prezzo Importante: A 550,81 €, rappresenta un investimento significativo. Costa più del doppio rispetto a un i5 di fascia media, quindi è giustificato solo se sfruttate davvero tutta quella potenza.

Consumi e Calore: La scheda indica "125 W di energia di base", ma sotto carico massimo (Turbo) il consumo sale drasticamente, generando molto calore. Non potete raffreddarlo con un dissipatore economico; serve un sistema a liquido o un dissipatore ad aria top di gamma.

Compatibilità Scheda Madre: Richiede una scheda madre con socket LGA 1700 basata sui chipset serie 700 o 600 (come Z790 o Z690). Se avete un PC di qualche anno fa, dovrete cambiare anche la scheda madre.

Esperienza d'Uso Tipica

Questo non è un processore per navigare su internet. È fatto per giocare a Cyberpunk 2077 con dettagli al massimo mentre contemporaneamente fate streaming su Twitch e registrate il gameplay in alta risoluzione. Per i video editor, riduce drasticamente i tempi di esportazione in 4K rispetto alle generazioni precedenti.

Conclusione e Raccomandazione

L'Intel Core i7-13700K è altamente raccomandato agli utenti "Pro" e ai gamer che cercano longevità e prestazioni assolute. Se il vostro obiettivo è solo il gaming in 1080p, potrebbe essere eccessivo (un i5 basterebbe), ma se lavorate con il PC o volete il top per il gaming ad alto refresh rate, è una bestia indomabile.

La Dritta in Più

Poiché è un processore della serie "K" senza dissipatore incluso nella scatola (la confezione è sottile e contiene solo la CPU), mettete subito a budget un dissipatore a liquido AIO da almeno 240mm o 360mm. I 13700K tendono a scaldare molto e un raffreddamento insufficiente ne limiterebbe le prestazioni (thermal throttling), vanificando la spesa extra.

I was comparing a Dell of similar spec to this one, but this one just won out for price point for what I was getting. I liked them so much, I bought two of them. One for the server, and one to use as spare testing Windows machine that didn't take up a ton of space (and wasn't a laptop).

Full Disclosure, I added a 500GB SSD NVMe M.2 drive as the boot drive, so your results may vary in terms of speed. But I will say, it was speedy with the stock drive that came with it (see below)

Here's what I liked..

- First off, who it came from. I was pleasantly surprised that the Amazon Certified Reseller that this came from (as the box said) is a company I know from my IT experience for decades. While they are a business2business company, many HP (and Dell) PCs I bought over the years, came from this company. So I know they know what they are doing. However, I can't say yours will come from this place, but have hopes that others are as high calibre as this one since they would be Amazon-certified also.

- This thing is small, its no bigger than a standard mouse pad.
- It's very clean, it almost looked new. No dents, scratches, or dings. The inside was spotless and the CPU had been remounted with fresh paste!
- Its powerful. I've done some hard video encoding and testing, and it just purrs along, and this was still with the included 500GB drive!
- It's quiet, unless I'm chewing the processor up with something the fans spin up. But even then it is not as loud as my desktop workstation (an HP also!).
- It's an energy sipper. I connected a power meter to it for a month, it used so little power (vs my desktop)
- Processor speed is pretty speedy and windows preinstall is pretty zippy on it
- This model has 16GB of ram which is plenty of ram these days for most applications
- Two drive support. This can take 2 drives, a 2.5" SATA drive & a NVMe M.2 2280 drive (just add a screw!)
- Plenty of USB 3.0 , 2 USB Type A (flat plug) and 1 USB-C in the front and 4 USB Type A ports in the back
- 2 Displayport ports for dual monitor support and a VGA port
- Onboard 10/100 ethernet & audio
- This specific renewed model comes with a Windows 10 Pro license! (some do not!)
- If you're security minded, this does come with TMP 1.0 and other UEFI related security tools.
- Since this is an HP Business PC, spare parts and support are easy to find and locate. Everything is HP standard, well tested, and made for years of reliability.

Here's what I thought was "meh"

- Because its tiny, the power supply is a brick on a cord. Not a big deal and the cord from the brick to the PC is long, but the brick itself has to be put somewhere vs a straight cord.
- This model does not come with WiFi or the antenna kit. The MiniPCIe slot exists though so Wifi can be added later and it's not a show stopper for me as these will be hard wired.

Here's what I didn't like..

None. I do not have any huge things I do not like about this product, other than my meh. I'm extremely pleased with this product!

Overall, as stated above, I'm extremely pleased with this product. Add a NVMe M.2 drive as your boot drive and you will be screaming for a low low price.

I ordered two of these. They were advertised as being refurbished by a certified refurbisher. These were going to be put in use as a continuous operation thin client, so i decided to double check the condition of the internals. I opened the case and on both units, the hard drive was installed incorrectly, and both were missing hard drive mount grommets. I pulled the heat sinks off the processors to check thermal paste. on the first, only 75% of the processor had contact with the heat sink from thermal paste, and the silicon thermal pads were falling apart and missing in some places. On the second unit, it appeared that thermal paste was applied by a stencil, however only about 50% of the processor was making contact because the heat sink was installed incorrectly, and the mounting screws were cross threaded into the chassis. This unit also had degraded silicon pads. I corrected the issues myself and put these in service. They are functioning well. Had this been left as provided, hot spots on the processors would have significantly impacted performance and shortened the life of the processors.

I did reach out to the seller and was offered a return authorization. I let them know that I corrected the issue, and it was pretty much left at that. I guess I expected something to cover my efforts to correct their failed attempt at refurbishing. I did ask if thermal management was something they addressed in their refurbishment process and did not get an answer on that. Being that I ordered 2, and both were in poor condition, I suspect this is the level of quality that can be expected.

I realize these are older units, and I would fully expect this quality from a private seller or surplus purchase, but I specifically ordered refurbished units to ensure they would serve the purpose I needed. I still think I got a good deal with this purchase, but understand, you will need some level of technical capabilities to ensure these meet the needs you have. Always check, because the issues above would quickly render these paperweights. Had these failed due to me not checking, the rating would have been 1 star, but because i was able to catch this ahead of failure, I saved the seller 2 stars on this review.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this mini PC for $209 and actually had very little expectations out of it at this price point. Also, in the past, products sold from this vendor contained Malware, so I was extra cautious and wary when I bought this item. But $209, who can argue with that. Especially with memory prices nowadays it’s ridiculous.

Anyway, first thing I did was go through the windows setup (without connecting to the internet…Important!) and installed Malwarebytes via USB key containing the full offline installer. Ran the scan…and it came up clean! No virus/malware found! This is good news as Acemagic had a stigma from issues with malware installed in past products, possibly compromising end user ho,e network security. This is good; great experience so far!

Since Windows 11 has a clean build of health, I deleted and wiped the entire drive so I can install Ubuntu Linux. I ran some extremely strenuous tests on this unit, and the cooling system is super impressive. I am running glmark2 (graphics chip benchmarking software) along with a stress utility that makes all 4 cores run at 100%. Even though with the heavy workload, this thing stayed relatively cool. The fan hardly runs. You can’t even hear it run. The glmark2 score was only 1269, so it is far from a hot rod, and having only a 4 core Ryzen 4300U CPU, you won’t be running large LLMs (for AI) on this, nor play any of the latest cutting edge games. Which is OK, because this unit isn’t for that. It’s for general purpose computing. And it’s oh so quiet! And doesn’t use up a whole lot of electricity, so you can have this running 24/7 with no issues. I’m planning to use this to run PiHole and Unbound (local DNS server), of which this K1 is overkill, since those apps were designed to run on a Raspberry Pi.

Just to set expectations, this is a very entry level machine meant to do general purpose work. However, you can still improve performance by doing upgrades on this (unlike any Mac hardware). If this is what you are planning to do, my suggestions is to get rid of that 256GB SSD drive. It is SATA and it is slow. Put a NVMe M.2 SSD 1TB or so. These newer NVMe drives are so much faster…bottlenecks are usually had in the storage drives, especially if you’re running an app that is using a lot of swap space in lieu of memory. You can actually leave the crappy SATA drive in there and install the NVMe alongside it (it has an extra NVMe slot in the unit).

Second thing to upgrade is the memory. This particular unit comes with 1 8GB SoDIMM module. There’s 2 slots available, so you can have up to 64GB memory in this.

All in all, I’m super impressed with this unit, especially at the price point. I highly recommend this for anyone doing general purpose computing and to play lightweight games (it’ll probably even run an Arcade emulator, like MAME with no issues!)

- does fit a 80mm fan with 4 screws on the side, or a 92mm fan with 2 screws and slightly cockeying the fan(ONLY IF YOUR GPU DOESNT EXTEND ABOVE THE TOP OF THE PCIE BRACKET)

Overall:

text:
I have a mid-tower PC I originally built in 2012 I wanted to resurrect for homelab experimentation. AMD FX-6100 (6 core, 3.3/3.9GHz, AM3+ socket) in an ASUS Sabertooth 990FX R1.01 motherboard with stock AMD cooler and upon booting it up for the first time in probably 8 years I immediately noticed the CPU temps were very high -- high 40s (C) at idle and exceeding 70C under load in under a minute, as reported by the motherboard BIOS sensor (probably the socket temp). The max safe temp for this CPU according to AMD is 70C. At a minimum I'd need new thermal paste but I recalled the CPU always ran hot with the stock cooler even when new so went looking for a replacement AM3+ compatible tower cooler.

Installation on my AM3+ motherboard was simple: remove the old cooler brackets from the motherboard backplate (mine is metal), screw in the new (included!) brackets to the backplate with standoffs, apply thermal paste to CPU, remove the plastic wrapper from the cooler plate and screw it down to the new brackets. Easy.

This cooler has exceeded my expectations. The CPU now runs high 20s at idle and won't exceed 42C at full load even after hours of stress testing, all at stock CPU settings. Overclocked to 4.2GHz at slightly higher than stock voltage it caps at around 46C and has been rock solid stable. (All temps from the BIOS/motherboard sensor reading.)

If you have an old AMD FX-series that's running hot like I had then this cooler is a great bargain. You could spend a lot more but why bother. It's also not easy to find a cooler that includes all the mounting hardware for AM3+ but this one does. Very happy with this purchase.

*** I didn't use the included thermal paste, I used ARCTIC MX-6, so I can't give an opinion on how well the included paste works.

text:
I bought this months ago, but amazon showed it in my history and I had not written a review for a product(s) I like and use daily. But as a 30 year IT person, I often have needs to find cheap PCs either for clients or myself at home.

Earlier this year I was in the market for a miniPC, as I wanted to use it as a server for my home network (running linux). Its me, so I didn't want to spend a ton of money, but wanted something decent, that I could upgrade. I'm familiar with this product line, as these are business grade computers, so I've used this specific model at companies (when these were new). In short, HP G-series PCs are pretty reliable, and last longer than their home ones. So no surprise they are for sale as refurbished on here.

I was comparing a Dell of similar spec to this one, but this one just won out for price point for what I was getting. I liked them so much, I bought two of them. One for the server, and one to use as spare testing Windows machine that didn't take up a ton of space (and wasn't a laptop).

Full Disclosure, I added a 500GB SSD NVMe M.2 drive as the boot drive, so your results may vary in terms of speed. But I will say, it was speedy with the stock drive that came with it (see below)

Here's what I liked..

- First off, who it came from. I was pleasantly surprised that the Amazon Certified Reseller that this came from (as the box said) is a company I know from my IT experience for decades. While they are a business2business company, many HP (and Dell) PCs I bought over the years, came from this company. So I know they know what they are doing. However, I can't say yours will come from this place, but have hopes that others are as high calibre as this one since they would be Amazon-certified also.

- This thing is small, its no bigger than a standard mouse pad.
- It's very clean, it almost looked new. No dents, scratches, or dings. The inside was spotless and the CPU had been remounted with fresh paste!
- Its powerful. I've done some hard video encoding and testing, and it just purrs along, and this was still with the included 500GB drive!
- It's quiet, unless I'm chewing the processor up with something the fans spin up. But even then it is not as loud as my desktop workstation (an HP also!).
- It's an energy sipper. I connected a power meter to it for a month, it used so little power (vs my desktop)
- Processor speed is pretty speedy and windows preinstall is pretty zippy on it
- This model has 16GB of ram which is plenty of ram these days for most applications
- Two drive support. This can take 2 drives, a 2.5" SATA drive & a NVMe M.2 2280 drive (just add a screw!)
- Plenty of USB 3.0 , 2 USB Type A (flat plug) and 1 USB-C in the front and 4 USB Type A ports in the back
- 2 Displayport ports for dual monitor support and a VGA port
- Onboard 10/100 ethernet & audio
- This specific renewed model comes with a Windows 10 Pro license! (some do not!)
- If you're security minded, this does come with TMP 1.0 and other UEFI related security tools.
- Since this is an HP Business PC, spare parts and support are easy to find and locate. Everything is HP standard, well tested, and made for years of reliability.

Here's what I thought was "meh"

- Because its tiny, the power supply is a brick on a cord. Not a big deal and the cord from the brick to the PC is long, but the brick itself has to be put somewhere vs a straight cord.
- This model does not come with WiFi or the antenna kit. The MiniPCIe slot exists though so Wifi can be added later and it's not a show stopper for me as these will be hard wired.

Here's what I didn't like..

None. I do not have any huge things I do not like about this product, other than my meh. I'm extremely pleased with this product!

Overall, as stated above, I'm extremely pleased with this product. Add a NVMe M.2 drive as your boot drive and you will be screaming for a low low price.

text:
I ordered two of these. They were advertised as being refurbished by a certified refurbisher. These were going to be put in use as a continuous operation thin client, so i decided to double check the condition of the internals. I opened the case and on both units, the hard drive was installed incorrectly, and both were missing hard drive mount grommets. I pulled the heat sinks off the processors to check thermal paste. on the first, only 75% of the processor had contact with the heat sink from thermal paste, and the silicon thermal pads were falling apart and missing in some places. On the second unit, it appeared that thermal paste was applied by a stencil, however only about 50% of the processor was making contact because the heat sink was installed incorrectly, and the mounting screws were cross threaded into the chassis. This unit also had degraded silicon pads. I corrected the issues myself and put these in service. They are functioning well. Had this been left as provided, hot spots on the processors would have significantly impacted performance and shortened the life of the processors.

I did reach out to the seller and was offered a return authorization. I let them know that I corrected the issue, and it was pretty much left at that. I guess I expected something to cover my efforts to correct their failed attempt at refurbishing. I did ask if thermal management was something they addressed in their refurbishment process and did not get an answer on that. Being that I ordered 2, and both were in poor condition, I suspect this is the level of quality that can be expected.

I realize these are older units, and I would fully expect this quality from a private seller or surplus purchase, but I specifically ordered refurbished units to ensure they would serve the purpose I needed. I still think I got a good deal with this purchase, but understand, you will need some level of technical capabilities to ensure these meet the needs you have. Always check, because the issues above would quickly render these paperweights. Had these failed due to me not checking, the rating would have been 1 star, but because i was able to catch this ahead of failure, I saved the seller 2 stars on this review.

This processor is on a completely different level from mainstream desktop CPUs. If you’re building a true workstation for heavy compute workloads, the 9995WX is an absolute monster.

The multi-core performance is honestly mind-blowing. For rendering, simulation, compiling massive projects, virtualization, or heavy multi-threaded workloads, it just chews through tasks. If your software can scale with cores and threads, this chip delivers in a huge way.

Despite the insane performance, efficiency per unit of work is actually very good when paired with proper cooling and a capable power delivery setup.

This is obviously not a chip for average users — it requires a proper workstation motherboard, server-grade cooling planning, and a serious power supply. But if you need maximum compute density on a single socket, this is about as good as it gets.

Man, pairing this chip with my EVGA RTX 3080 FTW3 was like dropping nitro into an already souped-up engine. The second I booted up, the system felt tighter, snappier—like it knew it had something to prove. Whether I’m gaming in 1440p ultra settings or messing around in Unreal Engine, this CPU pulls its weight and then some. It’s that perfect balance of muscle and finesse. Intel really went off with this one—those 14 cores (6 performance + 8 efficiency) are tuned like a street racer’s engine, ready to flip between chill and kill in a second.

I’ve got Chrome with 30 tabs, OBS streaming, Discord in the cut, and Spotify vibin’—and not once did it stutter. The P-cores chew through high-demand tasks, while the E-cores hold down all the background noise without breaking a sweat. This thing doesn’t even flinch when I alt-tab between Warzone and a 4K render preview in Premiere. It’s not just multitasking—it’s like everything’s running in its own lane, smooth and uninterrupted. I even ran a few benchmark stress tests just to see what would happen, and the temps barely nudged when paired with a solid cooler.

Speaking of which—let’s talk thermals. This ain’t a plug-and-play situation with any old fan. I slapped a 240mm AIO on it, and it runs cool even under heavy stress. You could probably get away with a beefy air cooler, but if you’re serious about squeezing out performance and maybe overclocking a little, liquid cooling is the way to go. That 125W base power ain’t just numbers—it’s a heads-up that this thing means business once all cores start firing. I also bumped the clocks up just to see how much headroom I had, and it stayed rock solid. Intel definitely gave us room to push without babysitting temps every two minutes.

It’s also built for the future. Running on a 600 or 700 series board, I’ve got full support for DDR5, which pairs real nice with my rig’s faster memory. PCIe lanes handled my NVMe drives and GPU setup with no drama. Everything just syncs like it was meant to be. No weird bottlenecks, no chipset hiccups. From boot speed to game loading to creative projects—it all moves fast and fluid, like you’re working ahead of the machine instead of waiting on it.

If you’re stacking this with something like a 3080, you’re basically setting up a power duo that can crush anything from AAA games to deep workflow projects without blinking. This CPU doesn’t just hold up—it leans in and asks for more. Feels like I finally unlocked the level where everything just works how it’s supposed to.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text: My stepdad-- who is not at all tech savvy -- needed a basic computer for checking his e-mail. He had been using an old laptop his sister had given him, growing more frustrated with its poor performance and overall lack of versatility, so I suggested he upgrade to something better. He did not need, nor was he interested, in a state of the art, hi-tech computer with all the bells/whistles, so I checked out the refurbished computers here on Amazon. This was my first time ordering a renewed PC and I took a leap of faith-- given my outstanding, years-long experiences buying from Amazon as well as the 90-day $$ back guarantee -- and ordered this HP ProDesk. Took it over to his house yesterday and set it up for him--WAHWAHWEEEWAH, I was blown away by how nice it was, especially for the price. It looked brand new. I had ordered a separate 27" monitor (will review that as well). Unboxing everything and setting it up took probably 15-20 minutes and consisted of mostly plugging in cables and cords. Although I still gave it 5 stars, it wasn't all peachy, however, so please be aware of the following: 1. The power cord is really short-- I think it was 24"? (I wish I had measured it), and we had to move his desk a significant distance to be closer to the wall outlet -- okay, an extension cord would have helped but stepdad just didn't have one on hand. 2. There was no HDMI port to connect the monitor to the computer -- we tried every port on the PC, to no avail. We figured out that the only way to connect monitor to PC was through a VGA cord-- not included with either the monitor or the PC. This necessitated a run to Best Buy where thankfully they had such a cord (you guys are the best!), $14.99 and yes, it worked perfectly. When that monitor screen lit up and displayed the Windows logo we both let out a whoop of joy, that's how good it looked. I went ahead and set up the starting questions for him and we connected the PC with the ethernet cable to his router (or was it the modem? not sure, but it worked) and he was in business. Absolutely fabulous, despite the 2 snafus we encountered with the short power cord and the lack of HDMI port on PC. Totally worth it, and I'm even considering chucking my old PC here at home -- which I purchased new, cost over $1000-- and "upgrading" to a computer exactly like this one. On an amusing side note-- the box that the computer came in is the perfect size for an adult cat to sleep in. As soon as I took the PC out and into the home office, within 5 minutes, Fluffy was in that box sound asleep, on top of the packing materials. Highly recommend this product! Even if you don't have a cat! :)

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I have been building/buying computers for forty years, starting with an Altair back in the day. My previous purchase in 2006 was a 64-bit Compaq/HP unit running XP, which I modified to a dual-boot XP/Win 7 machine. Though slow, it worked OK and I didn't give up on it until the BIOS failed recently, and it can't run Win 10. This guy is 4-12 times as fast (see Passmark CPU), with USB 3.0, four 6 GPS SATA ports and, last but not least, a virgin Win 10 (with its COA sticker on the side) which will be needed as Win 7 goes unsupported next year. An encouraging side note: Win 10 backs off a bit from the smartphone-like Win 8 interface -- though that's still lurking when you hit Start -- resembling Win 7 more than Win 8 did. You would pay over half the price of this machine just to purchase Win 10 alone.

Mine came with a 500 GB HDD and a SATA DVD reader, which I need to load my legacy software and photo discs. Two of the four RAM slots are stuffed to make 8 GB of memory. I'm not a gamer, but the Intel i5-4590 is quite competent; with more RAM, a video card in an open slot and an SSD in the empty drive bay, it should do fine. A new puter like this would run over twice as much. This one? Hard to tell that it's not new, it's that clean. And quiet. Since it was a business machine, it lacks two small but important touches: a WiFi connection and an XD card reader, which are cheap. I have two USB WiFi dongles already, and what with four USBs on the front (two are USB 3.0) and six on the back, there's plenty of ports. The HDMI outputs use HP's proprietary connector, so you'll need a special cable/adapter if they are used. There is also a VGA video OUT (won't see those much longer), which I use for my display as I'm already using its HDMI IN for DirecTV. (1920x1080 is the highest resolution supported by the integrated Intel graphics.)

In short: If you need an inexpensive, powerful and flexible Win 10 desktop to replace your old one, this is it.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
What I needed:
I needed a computer for my electronics lab. It didn't need to be immensely powerful, but I wanted something that would be easy to expand as needed. This PC met my needs almost perfectly, and at a very economical price. I purchased this 6 months ago (almost to the day), so this is not an "out of the box" impression, but one based on months of experience. It has been powered on (or sleeping) continuously, so I can remote access it when needed.

My uses are primarily centered around my lab work: Electronic Design, PCB Layout, and 3D Rendering of PCBs, along with Design of small enclosures and modest software development. I also have several PC connected pieces of bench equipment: Digital Scope, Power Supplies, Function Generator, and whatever thing I'm creating. Most of these connect via USB, and one via RS-232.

This PC:
You can see in the pictures that the front panel has 4 USB ports - 2 are SuperSpeed. These have already proven valuable for quick attachments.

The rear panel is loaded up with 6 more USB ports (2 of which are SuperSpeed), and I've used most of them. If I had to, I could easily dig out an old PS2 Keyboard to free up another USB port - but with 4 empty ports on the front I'm ok for now.

As noted above, I needed RS-232, and this PC had one - which is a bonus. Of course, I could have plugged in a USB to RS-232 adapter. Beneath the back-panel RS-232 port (the gray plug in the picture) is a VGA connector, which I don't expect to use. To the left of those are a couple of Display Ports - one connected to my big screen (3440 x 1440). The specs say that each can support a 4K monitor, but my bench doesn't have space (and the screen resolution works for my eyeballs and needs).

The host processor in the unit I purchased is an i5-4590 quad core running at 3.3 GHz. The motherboard memory slots are full, loaded with 16 GB of RAM. The motherboard has 3 SATA ports, but they are fully occupied, connected to a 240 GB SSD hosting Win10 Pro, a 1GB spinning HDD, and a DVD drive. The graphics is served with an integrated Intel HD 4600. For further expansion, there are 4 PCIe slots: 2 x X1, 1 x X4 and 1 x X16.

Other Discoveries:
* The BIOS still had the name of the prior "owner" (a company), which is probably where many of these came from. It was simple to change, so now is hosts a name appropriate for my lab.
* This PC is not for gaming, so I didn't rate that since I've never run a game on it. With my single high-resolution monitor connected, spinning a 3D model of a modestly complex circuit board is fast - it more than meets my needs.
* And I had no need for Tech Support, so I didn't rate that either.

My Expansion:
* In the pictures you'll see one of the PCI slots is occupied - with the 4-channel SATA adapter that I added. The 3 on the motherboard were occupied but I needed one more for an external HD dock.
* I expect to add a Webcam soon.
* I also expect to add one more PCI card to it, to add USB-C connectors. My newest gear (Laptop, Phone, etc.) all have USB-C, so this will be necessary.

My Summary:
This was the right PC for my needs. It was also relatively inexpensive. It has been running close to non-stop since my unboxing. It "seems" quiet enough for most any location, but my lab isn't the best place to judge that.

It didn't have support for every interface I needed but was more than expandable enough to add to it. I do wish the overall unit was a bit smaller (for my lab space), and in years prior I had a large tower PC, but tired of crawling under the desk to swap cables around.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
It was delivered on time and was in like-new condition as advertised. It has a smaller footprint than a full-size desktop which I had concerns about before I got it. However, once I opened the access panel, I was impressed. It has a recessed latched pull handle that removes the whole access panel exposing everything and no screws to unscrew or lose. Inside, not a speck of dust, literally, like a new computer, you can't tell that it's renewed/upgraded.

Even though it's smaller everything is easy to see and get to so if you need or want to do anything inside it's awesome. You can see everything and get to it with ease. You don't have to be a contortionist or have tiny hands and fingers. The drives and optical reader (DVD) are contained within a rack that you just pivot upward to release and you have full easy access to them. Additional expansion slots to add what you like. If you should want to increase RAM from 16 to 32 GB there is nothing around them so removing and replacing them in the slots would be effortless. I was surprised how cool this computer runs even when using multiple high resource software at the same time with no lag.

As for the USB Keyboard and Mouse, USB WiFi Adapter. These are low cost and just so you have something. As low cost as keyboard and mouse are I really like them. If you use something else don't throw them out as others have said. Save them as an emergency back up or give them to someone. I have a Logitech wireless keyboard and mouse but still using the ones that came with this computer. USB WiFi Adapter isn't the best it's not real fast and not great for long-distance so I did buy a better one at the same time. There are a lot of cheap USB WiFi Adapters that stop working after 2-3 months but here is a low-cost $17 good one I use so can avoid the hassle.
Just search amazon for -
TP-Link AC600 USB WiFi Adapter for PC (Archer T2U Plus)- Wireless Network Adapter for Desktop with 2.4GHz, 5GHz High Gain Dual Band 5dBi Antenna, Supports Windows 10/8.1/8/7/XP, Mac OS 10.9-10.14
It increased my transfer speed from 300 Mbps or less and 3 bars signal strength to a transfer speed of 433 to 490 Mbps and 5 bars signal strength.

All you have to do is connect a monitor, the keyboard, mouse, and USB wifi adapter and power up. You do need to set up you user account like any new computer. This is Microsoft so it wants you to use a Microsoft account to have a better "online experience". But all you need to do is enter your login for a Microsoft email account or create one during set up. That step requires connecting to the internet and entering the password. Or you can create an offline user account like the old days. The rest of the setup questions are about your preferences and you're ready to go.

Windows 10 Pro works perfectly. My daughter got one of these a while ago and wouldn't stop praising it so I got one. She gave me a heads up about the USB WiFi Adapter solution too. I couldn't be happier with this purchase.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This CPU was a monster when it came out. Intel was finally forced by Ryzen to put more than 4 cores on consumer chips and we got the 8700K and 9900K, two of the best CPUs ever for their respective eras. That Coffeelake was also the best IPC jump Intel had since Haswell made it a great platform. Both were fast enough to keep up for several generations. And being 8c16t, 9900K still has very relevant performance today. It still performs well in the latest titles excepting a few broken ones; especially so when overclocked.

All that being said this was where Intel started to hit the wall with 'Lake' architecture, and it is a fairly power hungry CPU. With even a mild overclock to 4.9GHz this chip uses around 180-200W to achieve what a 5700X or 5800X can do at 65W and 105W respectively. The Ryzen chips even outperform it in emulators and in many modern PC games.

Also, at the time anyway, this CPU was not a worthwhile upgrade over 8700K unless you had a specific use-case. The 8700K with an overclock got pretty much identical performance in most things and threw WAY less heat into the room. For me 9900K gave a nice boost in RPCS3 and a few compression related things and not much else. I ended up moving on from it earlier than planned and jumping to a 7900X3D. 3D V-cache gaming performance, combined with the high clock scaling of the non-3D CCD, in a 12c24t CPU makes it a perfect jack of all trades. Nearly twice as fast as 9900K in a few scenarios. That it can do all this at 120W makes the 9900K seem very silly indeed. Granted Zen 4 is a newer CPU by a few years, but that was the comparison I experienced. 10th and 11th gen only got hotter and more power hungry and Zen 4 spanks them pretty hard too.

I used this CPU to push a 3080 and then a 3080Ti at 1440p and it did the job wonderfully. I'd still be using it if it weren't for emulators. The 9900K still gave me top-tier performance in most dedicated PC titles and did workstation tasks very nicely. My 7900X3D absolutely mauls it in RPCS3 and Dolphin though. And those are applications where CPU performance legitimately matters and can make a difference between playable and unplayable.

Nowadays I wouldn't recommend buying this CPU new OR used. It's still expensive and you can match or beat its performance with a 5700X/3D or 5800X/3D for much cheaper, using less power, and on a platform with newer capabilities. If you can get it very cheap however, or are still using one, there's not an urgent need to get anything better. Particularly if you only use a mid-range GPU like a 4070 or game at 4K where the chance of a CPU bottleneck is less.

Let’s just say it up front: if you’re building a mid-range gaming PC, a light workstation, or even a home lab test bench, the Ryzen 5 5600 is still one of the smartest buys you can make in 2025. This chip came out as a "budget refresh" under the 5600X, but guess what? It performs 95% as well for less money—and that’s a win in my book.

I’ve used this in three different builds:

A gaming rig with a 3060 Ti and 32GB RAM (runs everything at 1080p/1440p like butter)

A micro-ATX NAS/media server combo

A test bench I keep at the shop with a stripped-down Linux distro for container dev

And across all of them? It’s stable, fast, and ridiculously power-efficient. The 6-core, 12-thread layout handles multitasking, gaming, streaming, compiling, and even light 3D rendering without breaking a sweat.

Why It’s a Beast (for the price):

Base 3.5GHz, boost up to 4.4GHz—plenty fast for any modern task

Unlocked for overclocking (though most people won’t need to—it's already well-tuned)

AM4 socket = drop-in upgrade for tons of older B450/B550/X570 motherboards

Paired with a decent cooler (like that Thermalright Assassin 👀), it runs cool and quiet

Works perfectly with budget DDR4—no need to jump to DDR5 yet

What Could Be Better:

Doesn’t include integrated graphics—so you’ll need a GPU, even just to boot

Not future-proof for AM5/DDR5 platforms—but that’s why it’s priced like a legend

Stock cooler is okay… but you’re gonna want to upgrade if you're pushing this chip

TL;DR:
The Ryzen 5 5600 is still one of AMD’s most balanced chips ever made. It’s affordable, reliable, snappy under pressure, and perfect for gamers and builders who care more about performance per dollar than flexing on Cinebench charts.

If you're building smart—and not just shiny—this is your CPU.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
If you want to build a "budget" gaming PC.... DO NOT! WITHOUT DOING SERIOUS RESEARCH

My review is directed towards gamers since you can run MS Word on a potato and if you do video production, the Core i-7 is the sweet spot.

Now breathe, relax your mind, and manage the excitement you have garnered from the prospect of not having to pay to play online with friends (ahem! plus-live-gold), SAVE UP an extra $100 - 150 and buy this processor. I bought the AMD X4 860k, then bought the Core i-3, and finally this i-5 in a 2 week period (returned the others).

Why? Because this is a much more superior CPU. It is faster, has 4 cores and a frequency of 3.20 GHZ. Also, it has integrated graphics (which is a plus weather gamers acknowledge it or not). If you want an unlocked sucker, get the 'K' version for an extra $20. I bought this because I exceeded my budget by about 30% (tee-hee). You are getting every dollar out of it. Not saying you are not getting a bang for your buck from the other processors mentioned, but after hours and hours of research, it only made sense to "Eat the extra cost" since I'll be doing content creation (I know, but the Core i-7 bleh-bleh-bleh). If you are in doubt, I recommend these YouTube reviewers to give detailed explanations of the or-15 6500

A special thanks to the YouTube Channels, Science Review, Digital Foundry, Hardware Unboxed, Austin Evans, JayZsTwoCents.
These Tech reviewers are professional and carry out extensive research and benchmarks for a wide variety of games. In fact, 'Hardware Unboxed' is my favorite because they run benchmarks for at least 12 - 20 different games! Crazy huh?

My thoughts:The year 2016 is winding down and newer titles will eventually show up: you do not want to regret not utilizing every aspect of your PC to enjoy the experience. A good example is the Division which is about to bring its player base up and release content all the way into 2017. even though you can use a NOT-Core-i5 processor to run it, the game's minimum requirement is a Core i-5 2400, which is also a very good CPU as well. Its even cheaper than this (you will save about $50 or more if you don't want to spend on this)

Here's my build for you to weigh the cost (PS I wasn't going for Shinny PC, but a powerhouse):

Rosewell Micro-ATX Case with 400W Power Supply: Initially $38 from Amazon;s warehouse deals. Got an extra 15% discount because it didn't come with screws, hence $33 Also 400W can power most GPU's but my GPU required 500W, so i bought another PSU :(

CPU: Core i5 6500 3.2 ghz: $203 - Ouch! To the wallet, but worth every single dollar. (If it goes on sale at a lower price, I still won't be mad)
RAM: Ballistix Sport LT 8GB Single DDR4 - $42.99
MOBO: Gigabyte LGA1151 Intel H110 Micro ATX DDR4 Motherboard GA-H110M-A - $49.99
GPU: MSI GAMING RX 480 GDDR5 4GB (it was the same price as an RX 470, so why not) - $199.99
PSU: EVGA 500 W1, 80+ WHITE 500W, - $35.99
Time: At lest 4-6 Hours
Miscallaneous: $45

All part prices are from Amazon.com at the time of this review.
My Hard Drive's were from my old computers and my monitor was also from an old PC as well. You have to understand, this is still under $700 if you add the cost of a monitor mouse and keyboard. It's twice the price of a recent console, but it will perform better. Plus, it is open ended (or "future proof" - don't lie the term). I can upgrade my GPU when the next Gen of consoles are released. And if I become a millionaire before then, I can upgrade to the Skylake's Core i-7 Even then, PC ports will be optimized for the masses!

CONCLUSION
You, as the potential buyer have to weigh the cost, but from my research, this is one of the better gaming PCs you can rig up right now. In fact, a pre-built PC with these components was selling for about $800 a few months ago.
So, if you are looking for a budget gaming Rig, ensure you have a strong CPU and GPU. Prices fluctuate, so keep an eye out to get the best value for your money.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This is a really nice motherboard and was an upgrade over my older & much cheaper B450 that I, by a tragic mistake, dropped (literally) and accidentally broke. Visually, this ASUS motherboard I’ve replaced it with is stunning, much nicer than my last motherboard with larger & better looking heatsinks.

For clarification, I bought the WiFi II version of this motherboard. Software-wise, well, I couldn’t get the WiFi or Bluetooth to work right away, but I found the required drivers included on a DVD. After inserting the DVD, there’s clearly marked drivers for the WiFi & Bluetooth. Unfortunately for me, the files didn’t seem to work in Windows 10 for Bluetooth, but it did for WiF, which was more important to me. Windows Troubleshooter couldn’t get the Bluetooth to work, and the drivers I tried from the ASUS website didn’t work either in getting Bluetooth to work. Anyway, it’s not worth returning over or going to great lengths to troubleshoot outside of the windows Bluetooth troubleshooter, as I had a cheap Bluetooth adapter I bought for $5 years ago, which I just plugged in and it worked right away. One of the first things I did also was disable the “armoury crate” auto-download in the BIOS. I thought that for a nearly $200 motherboard, it was strange there were even such bloatware options in the BIOS on top of included Bluetooth I couldn’t seem to get connected to anything. That was something I more expected out of a motherboard in the barely-over-$100 price range.

It’s still a 5 (or maybe 4 1/2) star motherboard to me because despite the two little complaints I have about the motherboard, it still functions very well, handling a Ryzen 7 3800X with my H100i cooler quite well while also looking great. The RGB lighting on the motherboard looks great. WiFi works very fast with the included drivers on a DVD. (Although, in 2024, I’d like to maybe see drivers located on a cool USB) I had more fan headers on the motherboard than I had fans, which was nice.

I am too old and too busy to be a hardcore gamer, but I do play some games. I was deciding between this cpu and a 6 core cpu. I ended up saving the extra money and going with this one. Boy was I happy I chose this one.

I overclocked to 3.6 in a few minutes. I didn't want to keep pushing it because I didn't have time to figure it out and my cooling isn't that great yet. But at 3.6Ghz temps were at 35 celcius. So there is definitely more room to run.

Everyday use for me is lots of tabs in Firefox, thunderbird, AIM, Windows Media Center, word processing, powerpoint, excel, and the occasional Call of duty running at the same time. This CPU handles it all quickly with no lag at all.

Things to keep in mind: KEEP YOUR COMPUTER BALANCED. Watch out for bottlenecks when building a computer. Many people think certain good parts suck because their computer doesn't perform as well after they upgrade a part. It could be just a crappy vid card or low ram or slow hard drive.

A good CPU is needed to make a good fast computer, but so is a good Vid card, lots of RAM, and I can attribute my applications opening super fast to my SSD. But the point is, my CPU does not prevent those other good parts from their performance and vice versa.

Ich habe den Prozessor dann gleich verbaut und er wurde auch sofort erkannt vom Bios, und auch das Betriebssystem hat die neue Hardware ohne Probleme angenommen, die Treiber aktualisiert, dann Neustart, und fertig.

Ich hatte mich für diese CPU entschieden, weil mein PC net der neuste ist, und weil 2 verschiedene Sockel akzeptiert werden, und weil ich nicht wusste ob mein PC die neusten Modelle akzeptiert, dieser hier gute Bewertungen hatte, wollte ich es nicht drauf ankommen lassen, habe mich für die Kompatibilität entschieden.

Auch in Sachen Stromverbrauch war ich recht unsicher, wegen dem Netzteil, aber es reicht aus, selbst unter Vollast.

Ich habe auch keinen PC mit ATX Standart, da kann ich net einfach alles drin verbauen, muss immer schauen was passt.

Die Leistung ist zwar für viele Leute schon sehr veraltet, aber ich brauche nicht soviel, der reicht mir! Das ist auch das gute bei AM3+, da kann man diesen hier bsw. auch noch auf neuere Plattformen verbauen, muss man nicht immer gleich einen neuen Prozessor kaufen.

Ich habe den kurz gestresst, um zu sehen wie heiß der wird, ob meine Kühlung ausreichend ist, und es sind ca. 60 Grad und steigend, also wer die Absicht hat diese CPU zu übertakten, der sollte sich mit einer Wasserkühlung anfreunden, weil der wird echt warm. Zum übertakten kann ich im Augenblick nichts sagen, da meine Plattform das net unterstützt, die CPU jedoch schon, weil es eine Black Edition ist.

TOLL AUF JEDEN FALL, DAS ÜBERHAUPT NOCH ZU KRIEGEN! Damit die Möglichkeit nen älteren Rechner aufrüsten zu können, ohne gleich alles neu kaufen zu müssen. Schöne Sache.

text:
Let me explain my title.
I don't doubt this will work flawlessly on a Windows, Linux, Mac, etc., system. I have not tried. My application is to put a remote head on an Amcrest NVR which really needs it's own monitor, keyboard and mouse. It has its own webUI but it's not the same as the console UI. There are things you can configure in the console UI that you can't do in the webUI. This little gem saved the day.

But, let's backup. I typically don't like to spend lots of money on things that you "set it and forget it, so I was looking at either this unit or the IP_KVM (around $70) and the JetKVM ($100). I decided to spend a little more for this product that looked more... DONE, and I am happy I did.

My first impression when I opened the box was, "This thing is a BRICK!". It has some heft to it. Seriously, it's more solid and heavier than it looks. As opposed to the IP-KVM, which looks like it's a cobbled breakout assembly in a 3D printed box. That's my blind opinion, since I did not purchase the IP_KVM product.

Hooking it up is pretty much a no-brainer. It really is, "if the connector fit, that's where it goes". The only 2 things that could confuse you is the USB-C splitter. However, one head has a thunderbolt on it, meaning the POWER plug. You'll need a user-provided USB-A to USB-C cable to connect to power. And the other head uses the included (short) USB cable that connects to the "target device" for keyboard/mouse emulation.

Once it was all connected, I accidentally swiped the display with a finger and realized it has a tough screen, albiet, it doesn't do much but shows device status, but that's a nice surprise.

I would give 5 stars for this product, however, I was under the impression this device is accessible via VNC, but it can only be accessed via webUI. That's ok. You just have to remember it's another device that is accessible by web browser.

text: Bought it for our new HTPC. Installed it in an ASRock Fatality B450 Gaming ITX/ac AM4 motherboard, since it supports this processor (but only 200GE, not 220GE or 240GE) right from the get go, no BIOS updates needed. Updated the BIOS to version 1.70 nevertheless. Works great. For those who are new to the AMD platform, be sure to install AMD chipset drivers first, and then Adrenalin drivers for the GPU. Don't bother with All-In-One packages, IMO. As far as the processor's performance goes, I did notice CPU usage spikes up to 70% when surfing, watching Youtube or installing software. So, don't expect too much from it. On the other hand, for occasional gaming (Rocket League tier of games, mind you) it does pretty well, I must say. I presume it will perform even better with older games (but not GTA IV, for instance - 30ish FPS with medium/barely high settings, but GTA is known to be a CPU hog, so that shouldn't suprise anyone). Hardware decoding of 4K Youtube videos works flawlessly, but it does utilize 30-60% of GPU, while CPU utilization is minimal (less than 15%). Used it with stock cooler for a few days, and it worked great even though it's installed in a pretty small In-Win IW-MS04-01 ITX case (not much room in there). Nevertheless, splurged on a Noctua NH-L9a AM4 cooler. Works even better. So, as far as CPU performance and price go (even though we paid premium price as far as 200GE goes - 61$), give it a go (especially if you can get it for 50$). Plan on replacing it with 2200G in the (near)future, though. Was too cheap to pay 35$ more for a 2200G. Nevertheless, not too shabby. Recommended.

text:
I do very little gaming but a lot of photo editing, and bought this as a direct replacement for my old (but otherwise adequate) Pentium Gold G5400 CPU, as the i5-9500 includes the AVX2 instruction set that the latest edition of Adobe Photoshop requires to run.

The i5-9500 was purchased from Amazon US but was delivered to my address in the UK in little more than a week which, given that this was immediately before Christmas, is pretty impressive. The product came in an OEM box stating "This is not Intel Original Packaging" and came without instructions. Nevertheless it is unused and appears to the the genuine article and is supplied with heatsink.

Swapping over the CPU's was straightforward as I ran the old Pentium Gold at 100% for 5 minutes to soften the thermal paste before removing the old heatsink. Once the new CPU and heatsink were installed I was able to crank my memory speed up from 2400 to 2666 in BIOS, as the new CPU and my old memory are both capable of this. Windows 10 recognised the new CPU without any bother and Adobe Creative Cloud went about updating my Adobe Photoshop to the latest version - all good!

Apart from now giving me the AVX2 instruction set, I'm blown away by the speed that the i5-9500 renders the preview thumbnails in Topaz Studio 2 - what used to take a good 10 seconds to render 4 preview thumbnails with the Pentium Gold can now be done in less than half a second - I'd say it renders around 20 times faster. But as I don't do much gaming I can't comment on its gaming performance.

I'm very satisfied with this product which came at a good price, and with the prompt delivery.

text:
I was searching for a Plex Media server upgrade to my aging and stuck-on-Windows-10 HP EliteBook, and my reseach brought me to this listing. This is the first time I've ever bought a PC refurbished, and also my first experience with SFF PCs like this one originally designed for business/commercial use (all my other PCs were consumer oriented). As with most refurbished products, you never really know what will happen and you just gotta trust that the company did their due diligence with it before selling it to you.

UNBOXING: Out of the box, the packaging is very generous and was basically more than enough to pad all the crucial components. It came in the super thick bubble wrap that made it impossible to rattle around in the box. The mouse and keyboard came in a separated box, and other accessories were in separate bags.

CONDITION: I don't know if I got lucky or maybe this company really does refurb items properly, but my unit was pretty much immaculate inside and out. No visible scratches or scuffs on the outside, and the inside was shockingly dust-free. The ports all looked perfect (usually they would get mangled or scuffed up from constant use), and the AC power adapter was equally as immaculate. Either way, I'm more than satisfied

BOOTING UP: Setting it up was was dead simple. Turning it on brings you to the "HP Secure Boot" screen and you load straight into the Windows 11 setup screen. It was definitely a good taste of the performance of this PC because it just blazed through the setup screens.

IN USE: The clean Windows 11 installation was definitely true, because there was basically ZERO bloatware pre-installed. After all the updates that it installed shortly after setup, getting everything up and ready for my Plex server use was incredibly fast and simple. The i5-8500T (which I specifically looked for in my research since this gen of CPU had the improved Intel Quick Sync), 16GB of RAM and the 256GB SSD are such a big step up.

Even after opening up various Chrome tabs, NAS software, and transcoding my media library fails to cause this system to slow down or run into any performance issue. The fan does spool up and the PC gets a bit warm, but unless you have this PC right near your face or you have it placed on your hands, you won't really notice it running.

ACCESSORIES: they were generous to include the mouse and keyboard, WIFI + BT dongle, and DisplayPort dongle in the package. While they all worked pretty well, I only ended up using the DisplayPort dongle and the WIFI + BT dongle ONLY for the BT. My own mouse and keyboard were better, and Ethernet will ALWAYS trump WIFI especially for Plex use.

The WIFI + BT is half-hit half-miss. The BT part works pretty well with no disconnects experienced, but the Realtek chip for WIFI using the archaic 802.11n standard; my Wifi speeds were limited to 140-160mpbs up/down For comparison, my gigabit Ethernet basically hit 980mpbs up/down. If you have an Ethernet connection available, I STRONGLY suggest you use it with this PC.

VERDICT: This PC and, by extension, this refurb company have definitely set the bar high because I am very happy with this PC. While long terms reliable is still up in the air, the fact that this SFF PC with an 8th gen CPU was basically in immaculate condition and runs like a $1000+ machine is impressive. I'll update my review if I run into any issues down the line, but for now, solid 10/10

text:
At one point in time this was one of the best budget processors you could get along with the 10400f, which was back in 2020 to 2021. We've moved past that era but this CPU can still hold its own.
The i5-10400 non-F at least comes with integrated Graphics, which can be useful at times.

I bought this to test a couple questionable lga1200 motherboards. The reason I picked the i5-10400 over the i3-10100 and i5-10-400f is because the price wasn't all that much higher than the i3 and this one comes with the iGPU. With the iGPU, I don't have to hook up a Graphics card to test a motherboard.

Would I buy one of these for a budget build today? No, I wouldn't. The only way I'd think of it is if I already have an lga1200 motherboard. Otherwise I would go with a newer 6-core processor which can usually be found for a similar price. I'd avoid 10th and 11th Gen processors, unless I had no other choice.

The stock cooler? No, I would not use that either. Intel should have included the stock cooler that has a copper base, and it would help if they used a beefier cooler to that is screw mounted. In the past, my side hustle was buying broken gaming PCs, and a number of those broken PCs had an Intel stock cooler that had become dislodged.

text:
Was able to snag this for about $150 before taxes on a random flash sale, and used it to upgrade my home theater PC, which I mainly use for VR and more casual titles at 4K in my living room.

For me, this replaced an aging i7-6700K. The performance uplift is night and day between the two, and this would make a fine chip for any new gaming PC you might put together today. Please note that the F variant does not have integrated graphics, but if you already have a GPU then this won't matter for you. This is only 6 cores, 12 threads as well. Being an 11th generation chip from Intel, there's no performance vs. efficiency core debate here, 6 cores is what you get.

One word of caution is that as I write this review this CPU is currently listed for $199, which is about the most I'd recommend paying for this CPU. The $150 price I paid was fantastic of course, but it's not something I would rely on getting again even with Black Friday/Cyber Monday coming soon. A newer i5-12400 will offer similar levels of performance for roughly the same or potentially less money, though that isn't overclockable. A 12600K would blow this out of the water, but you're looking at a far more expensive CPU. The Ryzen 5600 or 5600X are also great foils for this CPU, especially if they can be had for a cheaper price. The AMD chips also have the advantage of cheaper motherboards for that generation compared to the Intel chips at the moment.

End of the day, if you can get this for a good price, go for it, but this wasn't the absolute greatest even for its time, and newer chips can sometimes be had for a better price.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Got this for a new gaming rig I was setting up. The first Amazon package came as an empty box. The CPU box had clearly been compromised at some point at the Amazon Warehouse (I'd have to assume) and it had no CPU inside, only the documentation. Amazon was quick to send me a new one, and it wasn't a huge setback since I was still awaiting the motherboard and case. Second package arrived just fine.

You know what you're paying for here. This is a really high performance CPU with the capability to be overclocked to your heart's content, and (while nothing is "future-proof") it should stay relevant for a few years to come. Paired with a nice GPU (1070 GTX in my case) it's able to run literally anything I throw at it. Shadow of the Tomb Raider can run with nearly all settings maxed out/at high. It blasted through most stress tests I threw at it, and managed to score a 1456 on Cinebench's CPU test, hitting only 71 deg C at most.

This CPU (obviously) comes with no dinky stock Intel cooler, so I'm using a Corsair H100i v2 for cooling here, and it pays off in BOUNDS. I can OC stable to 4.9GHz (what I have it running at now) and it runs cooler, both at idle and under load, than my last CPU did with its beefy Coolermaster heatsink/fan. Albeit, the radiator fans can get a bit noisy at times, but I've been tweaking my OC profiles to reduce noise and I've gotten the noise factor down a bit.

Overall, I'm immensely satisfied. This is the first time (since the days of the 8800 GTX) that I've had a "relevant" gaming PC, something that can actually run modern AAA titles, and my quality of life has improved drastically as a result. No more FPS drops when I try and watch Twitch while playing Overwatch. No more stuttering and lagging when the OS decides to run some CPU-intensive garbage in the background while I'm gaming. It's pretty amazing.

Here's the full build, for anyone interested. I wholeheartedly recommend this build to anyone looking to upgrade or build their first gaming PC, and it's relatively budget friendly compared to pre-built options, especially if you can snag some or all the parts on sale:
Intel - Core i7-8700K 3.7 GHz 6-Core Processor
Corsair - H100i v2 70.69 CFM Liquid CPU Cooler
Asus - PRIME Z390-A ATX LGA1151 Motherboard
Corsair - Vengeance LPX 16 GB (2 x 8 GB) DDR4-3000 Memory
Kingston - A400 120 GB 2.5" Solid State Drive
EVGA - GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB SC Gaming ACX 3.0 Video Card
NZXT - H500 (White) ATX Mid Tower Case
Corsair - 850 W 80+ Platinum Certified Fully-Modular ATX Power Supply

Whole build totaled out to about $1,300 after mail-in rebates.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I’ve been using the Intel Core i5-10400F in my build, and it’s a fantastic processor for gaming and productivity. It delivers solid multi-core performance at a budget-friendly price, making it a great option for mid-range systems.

With 6 cores and 12 threads clocking up to 4.3 GHz, this CPU handles gaming, multitasking, and general productivity with ease. It runs modern games smoothly when paired with a decent GPU, and it handles light video editing and streaming without issues.

This CPU performs exceptionally well in gaming, offering frame rates comparable to higher-tier processors when paired with a capable GPU. It also handles multitasking (browsing, streaming, and gaming simultaneously) with no hiccups.

With a 65W TDP, it runs cool and power-efficient. Even under load, temperatures remain manageable with the stock cooler—though upgrading to a better cooler is 100% recommended as stock coolers usually are terrible which I'll explain later.

Works flawlessly with Intel 400 series chipsets and fits into the LGA1200 socket. Installation was straightforward, and the CPU was recognized immediately.

Issues you may want to consider before buying:
The "F" series lacks integrated graphics, which means you must use a dedicated GPU. This isn’t an issue for gaming setups but could be inconvenient if you’re troubleshooting without a graphics card. The included cooler is terrible, it’s not ideal for overclocking or heavy sustained loads, or even normal use. If you plan on pushing the CPU or just try and use it for gaming, you’ll want to upgrade to a better cooler. Since this is a non-K processor, it has limited overclocking potential. However, it still boosts up to 4.3 GHz automatically, which is plenty for most users.

Overall:
The Intel Core i5-10400F is a fantastic mid-range CPU that offers excellent gaming and multitasking performance for the price. It’s power-efficient, reliable, and affordable, making it perfect for budget-conscious gamers and general-purpose users. Just keep in mind that you’ll need a dedicated GPU and might want to upgrade the cooler if you plan on long gaming sessions or heavier workloads. Highly recommended for gaming rigs and productivity builds on a budget!

text:
Replaced an i5-8400 with this guy. Was good for the price, but I had to replace the cooler. On paper, this thing is supposed to handle things just fine (TDP for TDP). In reality...different story. I was monitoring system temps while performing basic tasks and they were always abnormally high (50C idle, 70C at 40% load). This was with the stock thermal paste.

I ended up having to take my rig back apart and inspected the surfaces for both my CPU and the cooler. CPU was smooth as butter. Cooler? Not so much. Saw a few gouges and a couple small pieces of metal in the compound. Hoping that I could compensate with a good thermal paste and verifying good application, I saw absolutely no change in temperatures. Sadly, the cooler comes bundled with the processor so best I can hope for is the AMD RMA process, which nobody has time for. Conclusion? Just get your own cooler, even if you get this processor. Hopefully mine was just messed up at the factory, but it wasn't cutting the mustard on light tasks, which means it would have been hurting under heavy load.

Thankfully, there is more than just the cooler in this package. The processor itself is, to put it lightly, in a different league than the 8400. Cold boot? 6 seconds. Shutting down? 2.5 seconds. Windows 10 installs faster than you can blink. It's more than sufficiently fast for my needs so far, especially coming from the experience I had with the 8400.

Apparently there's controversy around the 5700 being a 5700g with the APU disabled. Coming in from being an Intel guy for so long, I really have no basis for comparison. I ended up with a bunch more cores, threads, fabrics, rebars, gidgets, and gadgets than I had before.

For the price I paid, even with having to get another cooler, it's worth it. Would I have enjoyed a frustration-free experience for a few extra bucks? Heck yeah. That cooler was polished with a brillo pad and it almost makes me wonder if I was working with a refurb in disguise, but I digress. Still worth it. Now happy to be on team red.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Because video cards are so expensive this year, I could only update the RAM and CPU on my rig this year. I have an ASUS Z370-A motherboard and it’s listed as compatible, but when I installed the new CPU the computer didn’t boot. Troubleshooting said to update the BIOS which made sense because the BIOS I had was from 2018 before 9th gen Intel CPUs. Swapped the CPUs and updated the BIOS with the old CPU and then reinstalled the new CPU and it booted perfectly.

- Be sure to update your BIOS before you install the new CPU
- Only replace one thing at a time. I know it’s more work to boot up in between, but if you replace RAM, too, you won’t know what’s not working if the boot fails.
- Keep your old chip handy in case something goes wrong and you need to swap it out
- Don’t put too much conductive paste on the back. One instruction video said a drop about the size of a grain of rice. That seems right. Too much and it gets everywhere.

Overall, installation was pretty easy. It took me a couple of tries to get the orientation correct, but it only fits on one way. The hardest part, really was finding and downloading the BIOS on the ASUS website and attaching the Coolermaster radiator and fan over the top.

One note: This CPU comes with video but the HDMI out on the motherboard stopped working, It’s not an issue because I use the HDMI and DVI out from a 1070 video card.

Bottom line: it was a good upgrade. My games run moderately faster with better frame rate and nothing seems to be running hotter. I’d recommend.
