I’ve been using the Corsair CX650M in my build for a while now, and it’s been exactly what I hoped for in a solid, no-nonsense power supply. The semi-modular design is one of my favorite parts — you only plug in the cables you actually need, which keeps the inside of the case much cleaner and makes airflow better.

650 watts is plenty for most mid-range systems, and this unit handles things without breaking a sweat. It’s not crazy expensive, but it doesn’t feel cheap either. It has enough juice to run a decent GPU and CPU combo comfortably, and I haven’t had any stability issues, even when the system is under load.

Noise levels are low, which I appreciate. The fan stays quiet during normal use, and even under heavier load it doesn’t ramp up to an annoying level. It’s one of those parts that just does its job without calling attention to itself.

Build quality feels good too. Corsair has been around forever in PC hardware, and this PSU shows why. The wiring feels sturdy and the connectors are solid — nothing flimsy. It also has the 80 Plus Bronze efficiency rating, which means it wastes less power and runs more efficiently than basic units.

All in all, the CX650M is a dependable choice if you want a reliable power supply that’s easy to work with, stays quiet, and supports a wide range of components. If you’re building or upgrading a mid-tier gaming or productivity PC, it’s a power supply worth considering.

text:
The CORSAIR Sabre v2 PRO carbon fiber gaming mouse sits at the top of their gaming mouse lineup and naturally competes with the flagship mice from Logitech, Razer, and, in 2026, many other competitive gaming accessory companies. At 55g, this carbon fiber unibody mouse has an excellent fit and finish, as it should for a premium $279.99 price point that includes a quality braided USB-A to USB-C cable, an additional set of mouse skates, and grip tape, packaged in a nicely branded travel case with the USB-C 2.4Ghz Dongle.

With tri-mode connectivity, you can connect with the 2.4Ghz Dongle, Bluetooth, or simply wired using the included braided cable - though I think the cable would be a little weighty as it appears to match what Corsair provides with their keyboards. With polling rates up to 8,000Hz and a DPI of up to 33,000, it is customizable using a web driver that seems to be the choice of many gaming mouse manufacturers in 2026. I do prefer this lightweight web browser method to an App that takes additional processing overhead running in the system tray. You can also update the firmware, set up macros, along with other device settings, and I'd say the web driver matches many of the competitors in terms of its functionality.

The mouse feels great in the hand, with a size well-suited for a claw-type grip, though it is very, very smooth with the carbon fiber unibody, so the included grip tape is recommended. The Left, Right and Side mouse buttons are tactile and have a subtle click, not silent, though the scroll wheel is quiet. Battery life is quoted up to 120 hours using the 2.4Ghz Dongle at 1,000Hz; however, your mileage will vary depending on DPI and polling rates. I haven't had it long enough to get a good gauge on it at this point, but I hope it will be better than previous Corsair mice that haven't had a history of great battery life.

Overall, the Sabre v2 PRO gaming mouse from CORSAIR is a flagship mouse with performance to match; however, in a highly competitive gaming mouse market in 2026, honestly, there are models that match both the build quality and specifications at a significant savings in comparison. That said, CORSAIR generally offers discounts throughout the year, so I'd likely be more inclined to recommend this model more so when on a deal. Even the Sabre v2 PRO Magnesium version would be a likely recommendation with $70 savings, and really only lacking a travel case in comparison. Admittedly, while I'm a fan of CORSAIR and their gaming accessories, I do think price versus performance is a valid and important consideration, in my opinion. If price isn't a concern and you are already in the CORSAIR eco-system of PC and Gaming Accessories, well, the Sabre v2 PRO in carbon fiber is a solid option. Otherwise, I think you have options as I've noted.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Good: Just about everything. This is my first PC build in a few years, and it was pleasing to see that the state of the art has advanced quite a bit. The case is attractive without being garish, lightweight despite the glass panel but solid. Edges are deburred and painted, although there were a couple of rough spots in hidden places which, of course, I immediately found digitally while checking things out. The side panels are ridiculously easy to remove; two fasteners, tip the panel out and slide off. USB ports and controls on the top edge of the case. Two drive bays, which can probably accommodate four SSDs, set crosswise in the case because why not, I guess. I was briefly taken aback that there are no bays accessible at the front panel, but on reflection there's no real need for that nowadays. In their place, the entire front panel can be stuffed with fans if desired. There is certainly no lack of ventilation, large grilles in front, rear, and top (the top is covered with a nifty removable pet-fur and fluff filter,) and you can mount fans in all of them. It comes with one fan each in front and rear. The layout in general is logical and builder-friendly, cables almost route themselves. Comes with a handful of zip ties and a good assortment of fasteners. Very good price for what you get.

Bad: The supplied fans are a bit buzzy at full speed. I'm planning to add fans anyway so I might as well replace them. I'm also not a big fan (ha) of the glass side panel, even though that seems to be the style now. I'm not going RGB-happy and turning my rig into a scale-model rave club, so would have preferred an option to get this box with a regular steel panel.

Ugly: The shipping box appears to have been dropped rather hard on one corner. It was well-packed, so no visible harm done.

Bottom line: Considering that it isn't difficult to lay out $150 or more for a case nowadays, this is a great value. You get everything you need in an attractive, well-engineered package. If they'd used some Noctua fans to keep things quiet when the CPU/GPU get busy, it would be just about perfect. As is, I'm very happy with it. Five stars.

text:
Il CORSAIR 3000D AIRFLOW è semplicemente uno dei migliori case mid-tower che abbia mai utilizzato. Appena aperto si percepisce subito la qualità dei materiali: struttura solida, pannelli robusti e finiture impeccabili. Il design è elegante e moderno, perfetto sia per una build gaming che per una workstation pulita e professionale.

Il punto forte è ovviamente l’airflow: il pannello frontale a mesh fa passare una quantità d’aria enorme, mantenendo CPU e GPU sempre a temperature ottime anche sotto carico. Le ventole lavorano meglio e il sistema resta più silenzioso rispetto a case chiusi o poco ventilati.

Lo spazio interno è organizzato in modo intelligente: montare scheda madre, alimentatore e scheda video è stato semplicissimo, anche con componenti di grandi dimensioni. C’è tantissimo spazio per il cable management, quindi il risultato finale è ordinato e pulito, cosa che migliora anche il flusso d’aria.

Ottimo anche il supporto per il raffreddamento: si possono installare più ventole e radiatori senza problemi, rendendolo perfetto anche per configurazioni con raffreddamento a liquido. Il pannello laterale in vetro temperato permette di mettere in mostra la build e l’illuminazione RGB in modo spettacolare.

In sintesi, il CORSAIR 3000D AIRFLOW offre prestazioni termiche eccellenti, qualità costruttiva altissima e un design fantastico a un prezzo davvero competitivo. È un case che consiglio senza esitazione a chiunque voglia un PC potente, fresco e bello da vedere.

Assolutamente promosso!

text:
El Corsair 3000D Airflow es un gabinete de torre media diseñado para ofrecer una excelente refrigeración y una estética limpia y moderna, ideal tanto para jugadores como para usuarios avanzados que buscan buen flujo de aire y facilidad de montaje.

✅ Ventajas principales:
Excelente flujo de aire: Su diseño frontal de rejilla metálica permite una gran entrada de aire. Incluye dos ventiladores de 120 mm preinstalados, y tiene soporte para hasta 8 ventiladores en total, o radiadores de hasta 360 mm en la parte frontal y 280 mm en la parte superior.

Diseño limpio y elegante: Tiene una estética minimalista con líneas rectas, sin iluminación RGB de serie, lo cual lo hace ideal para setups discretos o profesionales.

Amplio espacio interior: Compatible con placas base ATX, mATX y mini-ITX, tarjetas gráficas de hasta 360 mm y disipadores de CPU de hasta 170 mm de altura. También permite hasta dos SSDs y dos HDDs.

Gestión del cableado eficiente: Tiene espacio detrás de la bandeja de la placa base para esconder cables y conseguir un montaje ordenado.

Construcción robusta: A pesar de su precio accesible, el chasis es sólido, con materiales de buena calidad y laterales de acero. El lateral izquierdo incluye panel de vidrio templado para lucir los componentes.

❌ Puntos débiles:

Sin USB-C en el panel frontal: Solo incluye puertos USB 3.0 tipo A y conector de audio combinado.

Sin ventiladores ARGB ni iluminación integrada: Puede no ser ideal para quienes buscan una estética gaming llamativa de fábrica.

Espacio justo para montaje de radiador superior: Si se instalan componentes grandes (como RAM con disipadores altos), puede haber restricciones.

text:
Das CORSAIR 3000D Airflow ist ein Mid-Tower-Gehäuse, das sich durch exzellente Belüftung, modernes Design und viel Platz für High-End-Hardware auszeichnet. Dank des luftstromoptimierten Mesh-Frontpanels und der großzügigen Innenraumgestaltung ist es perfekt für Gaming-PCs und leistungsstarke Builds geeignet.

Design & Verarbeitung – Schlicht, modern & hochwertig
Das Gehäuse kommt in einem minimalistischen, aber edlen Look mit einer Mesh-Front, die nicht nur optisch ansprechend ist, sondern auch für eine verbesserte Luftzirkulation sorgt. Die Verarbeitung ist hochwertig, und das Seitenteil aus gehärtetem Glas gibt freien Blick auf die Komponenten.

Kühlung & Airflow – Perfekt für High-Performance-Builds

Bereits enthalten sind zwei vorinstallierte 120-mm-Lüfter, aber das Gehäuse bietet Platz für bis zu 8 Lüfter oder 360-mm-Radiatoren für Wasserkühlungen – perfekt für leistungsstarke Systeme mit starker GPU und CPU.

Platz & Kompatibilität – Viel Raum für leistungsstarke Hardware

Kabelmanagement & Benutzerfreundlichkeit
Das Gehäuse-Layout ermöglicht sauberes Kabelmanagement mit vorgelegten Kabelführungen und viel Platz hinter dem Mainboard-Tray. Die abnehmbaren Staubfilter sorgen für eine einfache Reinigung und Wartung.

Fazit – Perfektes Airflow-Gehäuse für Gamer & Enthusiasten
Das CORSAIR 3000D Airflow überzeugt mit exzellentem Airflow, großzügigem Platzangebot und hochwertiger Verarbeitung. Wer ein gut durchdachtes, modernes Mid-Tower-Gehäuse für Gaming & High-Performance-Builds sucht, ist hier genau richtig!

✅ Vorteile:
✔ Starke Airflow-Optimierung mit Mesh-Front

✔ Hochwertige Verarbeitung & edles Design mit Glas-Seitenteil
✔ Gute Kabelmanagement-Möglichkeiten

❌ Nachteile:
✖ Nur zwei vorinstallierte Lüfter – zusätzliche Lüfter für optimalen Airflow empfohlen
✖ Keine USB-C-Frontanschlüsse (nur USB-A)

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Basically, this is the RM850x PSU with Taiwanese caps instead of Japanese caps. It's a B+ to A- tier PSU in most reviews, and is 0db capable at low temperatures, with a low noise fan. But it has ONE problem...it comes with 3 CPU power cables. THREE. But only 2 PCIe power cables.

This is ridiculous!

WHO needs THREE CPU power cables? I'll tell you who: NOBODY! CPU power cables #2 and #3 are completely pointless. There's not a mainstream or high end motherboard that needs 3. And even those that can use 2 really only need 1. However, there are dozens of mid to high end GPUs that require 3 PCIe cables.

I hope they update this PSU to include 2 CPU power cables and 3 PCIe power cables in the future. That would actually make sense.

All things considered, this is a quality PSU with a good price while still maintaining good quality. Solid 4/5 rating in my book.

When it comes to DDR4 RAM, dollar for dollar, this RAM upgrade is perhaps among the best. Sure, it's nearly $80.00 for two 8 GB sticks of DDR4 RAM, but you get what you pay for here. It's less expensive than some similar RAM while providing plenty of free random memory to your computer to run multiple applications at once or in the background. It does its job well and fast.

**I have seen a lot of confusion regarding RAM usage online, so let me clarify this here:

You can use all 4 RAM slots with this, too, which could stack you up to 32 GB of RAM; more than you would ever need.

You can use two DDR4 RAM slots in two same-colored channels on the motherboard, and pair it with another pair of DDR4 RAM sticks, whether they're 4 or 8 GB sticks, and they will work just fine together. Just make sure they run at comparable Megahertz (Mhz) levels, and that the stick pairs (for this paired Ripjaw type of RAM, and the other pair of RAM sticks) are in channel 1 and 3, and 2 and 4, respectively. If you use them any other way, you will cause the RAM to not run as fast or efficiently as it could.

End my little rant/lesson about RAM.

tl;dr:

This RAM is some of the DDR4 money can by, both for the price you pay and speed it provides your computer. I personally advise using it.

When I buy a headset I have 4 basic requirements.
1. Durability= metal headband solid padding etc. Doesn't matter how good the sound is if the band breaks off.
2. Comfort= if I'm going to wear this for 5 or 10 hours I'd like my ears to nor hurt like hell after basically.
3. Features= this includes stuff like, removable or adjustable mic, volume and mute buttons, coaxial audio jack or usb etc.
4. Price= I'm willing to spend the extra money for quality, to a point.
I've had these for little bit over a month and they still feel very cheap. I bought both the CPU & NVME water blocks, but it only lets me have 1 review.
NVME WATERBLOCK REVIEW.
It is fabulous at keeping the Samsung 980 Pro temps below 40 degrees. It was a tight fit to install the drive.
Located in the top slot where there is no air flow, my 960 evo was running solid at 80 degrees basically at idle. It was trapped between the graphics card and the water block just cooking. I bought this and the 980 Pro to replace the drive and improve thermals.
The 960 was placed in a heat sink and moved to where ther is good air flow and now maxes at 41 degrees.
Hooking the corsair nvme water block into the loop was a royal pain as it threw out the flow and was incredibly close to the cpu block. It was worth it for the temps.
Corsair's custom cooling has been really good. Their 360 rads have had little debris and made for the initial cleaning, CPU WATERBLOCK:
I bought their 1200/AM4 waterblock and it cools well enough, and wasn't as big as the previous cpu waterblock.
It can be rotated so that the inlet is at the bottom and the outlet at the top so the air bubbles can escape.
It is pretty light, and easy to install. There is not a large acrylic top, and the fins are not bent.
The lighting is great and works with MSI mystic lighting.
I used MX4 for paste. The temps are only 1 degree cooler than the previous water block.
It keeps my 5900X below 80 degrees for extended use.
It doesn't feel premium with all the molded plastic, but it does look good.
I trust corsair and their products and I hope not to have any leaks. I'll update if things change.

I'm happier with the nvme waterblock over the cpu water block.

CORSAIR Hydro X Series XM2 M.2 SSD Water Block Review
Introduction
Finding the perfect cooling solution for high-performance NVMe drives can be a challenge, especially with the advances in technology pushing the limits of heat dissipation. This review delves into the effectiveness and performance of the CORSAIR Hydro X Series XM2 M.2 SSD Water Block, which promises to keep even the hottest drives running cool.
Prelude to the Hydro X Series XM2
My journey began with a FireCuda 530 Gen 4 drive, which served me well but didn't fully utilize the capabilities of my B650 motherboard's Gen 5 NVMe drive slot. Eager to push my system's performance, I upgraded to a Crucial T700 1TB drive.
However, as I monitored the temperatures of my Gen 4 drive with the motherboard's stock cooler, it became evident that the existing cooling solution wouldn't suffice for a Gen 5 drive. The new motherboards might have larger heatsinks, but I needed a more robust solution to prevent throttling and ensure optimal performance.
Exploring Alternative Cooling Solutions
To address this, I experimented with the JEYI M.2 2280 SSD Heatsink Cooler, purchased from AliExpress. Despite its affordability, this heatsink delivered impressive results. During the CrystalDiskMark 1GB setting test, temperatures peaked at 56 degrees Celsius. While idle for 10 minutes, the temperatures never dropped below 45 degrees. For its cost, the JEYI heatsink was an outstanding performer.
My system, renowned for its extensive water cooling setup, includes a GPU that never exceeds 35 degrees Celsius while gaming at 4K 144Hz, with water temperatures at 32 degrees and ambient temperatures at 23 degrees. Although tempted to water cool my RAM and SSD, I refrained as my RAM, even with RGB lighting, never exceeded 49 degrees.
The CORSAIR Hydro X Series XM2 M.2 SSD Water Block Experience
Ultimately, I decided to try the CORSAIR Hydro X Series XM2 M.2 SSD Water Block. The results were promising: during the 1GB test, maximum temperatures reached 50 degrees Celsius. The subsequent 2GB test recorded 51 degrees, and the 4GB test also stabilized at 51 degrees.
The Hydro X Series XM2 demonstrated consistent performance and maintained lower temperatures compared to traditional air cooling methods. This water block is particularly beneficial for users with existing water cooling systems, providing a seamless integration and enhanced thermal management.
Considerations and Recommendations
For those experiencing issues with the CORSAIR Hydro X Series XM2, it's essential to consider several factors. Proper installation and configuration are paramount. text:
I bought these fans (2 sets of 3) because they have the extra set of reversable blades, which I wanted for a show-piece build. The supporting frame of the fans won't show when using them for intake fans, when you change to the reverse blades. Bottom Line I highly recommend them if you are controlling your fans from the motherboard's PWM and ARGB, and not using the "controller" others' have complained about. I have nothing bad to say about the controller, it is just that I did not need it for my build, since my Z690H motherboard controls and syncs PWM and ARGB for all fans.

The fans are well built and solid; they light beautifully and run smoothly; and they are quiet at low to medium speeds. At full speed (my testing) they can be heard, but I cannot imaging needing to ever run them that fast.
I also like that the fans swap easily - without tools - between forward and reverse blades. Also, the fans connect to each other magnetically, as well as the cables connecting magnetically.

Now to the only minor installation issue. Some others have alluded to it also. If you do not get the magnetic cable connector aligned perfectly to the fan, the pogo pins on the fan don't connect to all the tiny disks on the cable, opposite each pin. My first install, the fans were Dead - no spinning or lights. So, I needed to "wiggle" the connector around to get it aligned. It took me about six tries on one fan, to get the alignment correct, because the magnets are so strong they tend to pull the parts together quicker than the alignment can occur. This is NOT a reason to avoid these fans, I see the strong magnets as a good thing because once you get the alignment correct it isn't going to move. I also had the same mis-alignment with the magnets coupling the 3rd fan to the 2nd, until I simply "wiggled" them to align perfectly. THERMALTAKE should take note, and do a little redesign work so the magnetic connectors work more precisely, else they may get some complaints and returns, from unaware buyers, that the fans just don't work.

Bottom line is, I really like these fans and the are my new 1st choice for reverse blade fans.
Highly recommended !!!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text: Ordered a Corsair MP700 PRO XT 1TB to evaluate and setup at one of the workstations. At first glance and most notable is that besides requiring a heat transfer pad and heatsink out the box (not included with this model) this SSD will also require a dedicated PCIe 5.0 NVMe slot in order to achieve its full advertised speeds. Otherwise it will be severely bottlenecked if paired with anything lower end or lesser than PCIe 5.0 standard. Ex. a PS5 can only support a maximum top read speed at 8GBPS or about half of this drive's top 14.9GBPS read space. If used with an external enclosure the bottleneck will be the adapter's chipset and thunderbolt 4 port. Needless to say my test system only had 1 dedicated PCIe 5.0 slot for NVMe already in use by the OS and one other available shared one, so some compromises had to be made during testing. When copying and transferring files the bottleneck or max speed was determined by the source drives.. ex. C has a top speed of 7.2GBPS so can't copy faster than that to the target. When reading at 14.9GBPS or greater than 7.2GBPS the perceptible difference is nearly null except for very large files or some demanding applications ex. running local AI models. Otherwise, for daily common tasks or casual gaming this drive maybe currently faster than what any consumer reasonably needs. (For full diagnostics or to update the drive's firmware Corsair's SSD Toolbox software is recommended.) A bit pricey, but overall a fair deal at MSRP for top of the line performance for those power users who actually need it.

Ordered late Monday, arrived Thursday along with 4 other components using standard shipping. The remaining all showed up Friday. As usual, Amazon did a great job combining orders and I paid maybe $30 shipping in total, for everything. I installed the following, and this part was compatible:

ASUS P8Z68-V/Gen3 motherboard

Antec Nine Hundred Two V3 case
Corsair 60GB Force Series 3 SATA III 6Gb/s 2.5 inch SSD

WD Caviar Black 500 GB SATAIII 7200 RPM 32 MB cache OEM

Windows 7 64 bit OEM
Corsair Vengeance Low Profile 8 GB PC3 1600 mhz DDR3 memory
My old WD HDD SATAII 7200 RPM from previous PC
MSI GeForce GTX560 Ti 1GB DDR5 Twin Frozr II OC

This works nicely with my mobo setting on XMP. Fit nicely in the slots, sturdy and solid. Booted right up with no memory errors.

The thing I liked about these sticks is that it fits nicely under my CPU cooler with no clearance issues. I think the extreme epeen fins on some of the RAM may look fancy, but may not clear your CPU cooler if you're using air cooling. Particularly if you try to slot them in the first slot next to the CPU. These low profile barely clear the fins on the hyper 212 when put in slot one, in this mobo. So if you're considering buying the taller sticks, take this into consideration.

I'm overclocked to 4.5ghz with two 120mm front fans, 1 120mm rear fan, and a 200mm top fan and my mobo and cpu temps are barely above room temp at idle and never come close to any danger zone even at max settings stress testing using Intel Burn Test. I may receive flames for this, but that leads me to conclude that the finned RAM sticks are pretty much for show.

Great value, great name brand, would highly recommend this RAM for your overclocked air cooled rig, or any other set up for that matter.

Cheers.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I chose this memory for my first build because it was cheap and from a well known brand. I also liked that it didn't have the big heat-sinks like on the regular Vengeance RAM which allows room for aftermarket CPU heat-sinks. My PC is used mainly for gaming and Netflix, and 8 GB is more than enough for those needs. The only problem I had was the BIOS detecting them as 1333 mHZ instead of 1600, but a quick change in the BIOS fixed that that. Changing the frequency to 1600 mHz also increased the timings from 9-9-9-24 to 11-11-11-2?, so i had to manually change them as well, so be on the lookout for that. The timings issue is from my BIOS though and says nothing bad about the RAM. It works flawlessly; definitely recommended.

UPDATE (28 Dec. 2012): No problems after more than a year. I eventually brought the frequency back down to 1333MHz and was able to tighten the timings to 7-8-7-22. Stable, no problems.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Some keynotes for these fans:

**Edit: mounting these fans face down and running above 70% rpm causes the fans to rattle. Any other mounting position is fine
1) price: great value compared to other RGB loaded fans. You can get 6 for the price of 3 Corsair ll120 fans. And these fans are as good if not better than those.
2) authenticity: these fans do in fact run anywhere from 1850-1975 RPM according to motherboard reporting.
3) performance: these fans have more static pressure than other case fans which is better for getting air through case ventilation punchouts and dust filters. Have not tested on a radiator, however. I reccomend other fans for radiators anyways.
4) installation: much much better than Corsair RGB fans but not the best as far as cables go. You can either hook up the RGB to your motherboard (3 pin rgb headers) or plug into the control box that comes with the 3 pack of fans. I use my motherboard. Works as expected.
5) appearance: the RGB is very pretty. The reds are a little more dim than the rest of the lights but that's very normal and it's not distracting. Lights are bright but not blinding. Colors are pretty vivid. The blending of the light is also pretty good too. You have to really try to be able to distinguish where the individual LEDs are in the rings.
6) asthetic versatility: these fans look good wherever you put them or angle you look at them. I have the lian li o11d XL and I have these fans on the bottom serving as intakes. This means you see the back of the fan instead of the front. Usually that means you can't see any of the RGBs and it looks ugly, but these fans have the rgb rings on the back as well and makes the fans MUCH more bearable to look at from the back of the fan. If you have a case with bottom fan mounts, I especially recommend these fans if you care about that noice PC asthetic.
7) longevity: I expect these fans are not gonna have a great life expectancy given the price and MTF rating of 160k hours or whatever. Fortunately, these fans are cheaper and less bank breaking to replace.
8) quality: despite my lower expectations for longevity, these fans look and feel very good quality.
Overall, I'd highly reccomend these fans for anyone who doesn't want to spend Corsair money on fans. Despite what you might read in other reviews, I believe these fans to be very good for the money especially.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I know you, because you're me. You have a shiny new radiator which came with one or more perfectly functional fans, but you're now wondering if you can get an extra two or three degrees of performance out of your machine.

So you started looking into the wonderful world of fans. You now know that there are many types of fans and you figure that if you're gong to do this, you're going to do this right. So you want static pressure fans. Somehow you learned about Noctua: well-engineered, quiet fans that your favorite YouTubers rave about. They're ugly as sin, but you've come to appreciate their ugliness as a mark of exquisite Austrian quality.

THESE fans are not THOSE fans. They're well-engineered, yes. But unlike their retail sisters, they come in a classy black color. And they certanly are not quiet at 3000 RPM. I agree with the guy below who said he could barely hear himself think. I have two of these mounted in push-pull on a Corsair H60 AIO radiator. Anything above 1800 is kind of annoying. Anything above 2000 RPM is obnoxious. At 3000 RPM my PC sounds like a like a Ferrarri, which is nice, but I can't imagine running them at full speed for any period of time. But let's be honest: you really shouldn't expect a static pressure fan at 3000 RPM to be "quiet." That said, at 1500 RPM the fans are pretty much silent -- comparable to the retail version. Austrian engineering wins again.

Performance? They work as advertised. At full speed they move a lot of air. But if you've studied any thermodynamics you know heat transfer into moving air very quickly hits the law of diminishing returns. Put simply: more speed does not necessarily equal more heat transfer. At 1500 RPM it's about 1-2 degrees cooler than two stock fan at full speed (not bad) and is much quieter. There isn't much of a temperature improvement when ramping up to 2900 RPM, but it does get much louder (see above).

So if you insist on buying these, you might as well run them at 1500 RPM. But on the other hand, if you're going to keep them below 1500 RPM at load then why bother with the server-grade iPPC version? Why not get the iPPC 2000 RPM version? Why not buy the retail version which is a couple bucks cheaper?

You've already dug this far into a stack of Amazon reviews, so you're still seriously considering it. You know why and I know why. You're impressed by the numbers: THREE THOUSAND RPM. >100 CFMs. > 7 mm H2O of static pressure. 150K hour lifespan (that's 17 YEARS of continuous operation). And IP52. I'm not sure what that means but I suspect the fans will outlast the apocaylpse.

Is it worth it? Probably not. But you want these fans for the same reason you installed the water cooler and for the same reason you kept adding to your overclock. You want every ounce of performance. You want every degree of coolness. You want to press your machine to the limits. You can't imagine a situation where you'd need this kind of airflow but you like knowing that it's available.

You can use #6 32 1-1/4" screws to mount them to your radiator. Don't forget the washers. You're welcome.

edit: Ladies and gentlemen, I am writing from the future - May 2020. The apocalypse has, in fact, come. (Perhaps it is worth mentioning that I am a resident physician, and during these trying times gaming gives me some relief.) Many parts of the machine have been upgraded in the months since my original review, but the fans remain. And they still work. Stay home. Save lives. Be sure to wash your hands.

edit 2: it is now December 2025.

In the years of since my original post I have upgraded my machine multiple times. Most notably my i5-4790K was replaced by a i7-9700K in late 2020. Most recently I have left the small-form-factor SUGO SG05 and migrated to a roomy Silverstone FARA R1. Of course, this means I was able to upgrade my aircooler to the new champ, the Thermalright Peerless Assassin 120 Digital.

Temperatures improved, but I was unsatisfied. Do you think I replaced the PA120's stock fans with my iPPC 3000s? YOU BETTER BELIEVE I DID. (Did you ever doubt?)

With the iPPCs on the PA 120, idle temperatures are slightly above room temp (21 C), which is about five degrees cooler than stock. At full OCCT load, with fans running at full power, the CPU sits at 72 C - a full 10 C BETTER than the PA 120's stock fans.

I remain impressed. However! Since 2018 I have gotten married and now share an office with my lovely bride. And loud fans are actually a significant concern. I will therefore be upgrading to NF-A12s at the earliest convenience. Hats off to Noctua for an excellent product that continues to impress. I stand by my original review. If you want MAXIMUM POWER, these fans will give it.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I love these fans! I was hesitant to order them because of some reviewers saying they're horribly loud and others saying they were quiet. I was willing to take the risk and bet on the fact that those complaining they were too loud just didn't take any time to configure them, and I am so glad I did!

I installed 4 of these 140mm fans and 3 120mm in my new rig and I absolutely love them. I have 2 140's as front intake, a 140 as rear exhaust, a 140 as bottom intake next to PSU, 2 120's on my H100i radiator and a third 120 next to the radiator as exhaust. They all come with rubber brackets and I installed all but the radiator fans with Cosmos rubber rivets. Super easy! They all come with rubber sleeved cables that aren't too short and aren't too long. I did have to run a y-splitter for my two front fans because I ran out of pins on my motherboard, and it was enough of an extension to help them make it across the huge case to get them plugged in. If you have a large case and intend to put these near the front of your chassis, you will most definitely need extensions so plan ahead! I'd rather have to extend one set of fans than have 7 fans with super long cables cluttering things up.

After the quick and easy installation, I powered everything on and I was shocked at how loud it was. It was loud enough that my 10 year old and I had to raise our voices to hear each other clearly when sitting 4-5 feet away. HOWEVER, using ASUS' UEFI on the Maximus VII Hero motherboard, I was able to use the built in Qfan to quiet them down enough to the point that I could tolerate sitting near it while I installed the OS.

Once Windows was installed, I installed AI Suite (included with my motherboard, you may need to locate another fan controller if you don't have an ASUS board) and went into fan setup. It has 4 predefined modes to choose from with further customization possible if desired. Silent mode literally turns off all fans except the CPU fan, which it turns down considerably and the entire rig is dead quiet. Standard mode is a step up but still extremely quiet, even when sitting only 2-3 feet away. When on the other side of the room playing games on the TV, I don't hear it at all. The other two settings include turbo (around 1500 rpm) and full power. When all fans are running at top speed (about 2700-2800 rpm), it is extremely loud. Turbo is tolerable. The sweet spot is around 900rpm, which is enough to keep an EVGA GTX 980 Ti under 60 degrees while gaming and keeps my i7-4790k under 40 degrees, even under load. The result is a very stable, quiet and cool rig. I haven't found anything that can cause this system to break a sweat and I attribute it largely to these fans.

I am so very pleased with these fans, I can't say enough good things about them. They are roughly twice as expensive as other popular fans, but I'd much rather take the cool, quiet performance of Noctua fans than have fancy loud LED fans in my rig. I'll definitely be picking up more Noctua's when I build my husband's rig next month.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I just built my screaming Ryzen9 beast of a PC with a dual 120mm Corsair AIO. I foolishly figured I could cool the volcano that is Ryzen9 with minimal noise on a dual radiator. Not only could I still hear a slight whooosh from the stock Corsair fans at their lowest controllable PWM speed, but the CPU temps floated at 47-52C idle. I tuned up my fan curves to keep things relatively quiet, but anything over 400rpm on the stock fans was audible.

Worse yet, when I blasted the CPU with some full load tests, the case damn near took off and flew out of the room. Temps settled at a max 72C, but the fan noise was punishing. It is rare that I will ever get a full 24core load like that, but... I still have to know the limits of my system, right?

Annoyed... I hit Youtube. Linus always uses Noctua fans and I kind of figured that was just product placement, not really performance based. How much better could Noctua fans really be...? The Amazon reviews just seemed like an exercise in cognitive bias: "Well I paid $100 to swap all my fans to Noctua, so they must be better... duh!" I've been building PCs for 20 years and I have always tried to stay away from 120mm fans in favor of larger 140mm (or even 200mm when my cases allowed). Bigger fan = slower speed & less noise for the same amount of air. At least, so I thought...I swapped the two front 120mm fans on the AIO for these glorious NF-A12's and I was shocked at the difference. SHOCKED I TELL YOU!

Before I modified any of my fan curves, I noticed the idle temp average dropped about 2C--no tuning changes, just the new fans. However, that was running the AIO fans in the 400RPM range. I played with the PWM and discovered that anything under 1000RPM these A12's are pretty much inaudible. Therefore, I picked my idle setting up to ~800RPM. I can't hear a damn thing sitting at my desk, BUT... my idle temps are down to 38-42C. All I hear is the gentle whine of the AIO pump on its lowest setting. Seriously, its absolutely amazing how quiet these fans are. I honestly got down on my hands and knees to figure out if the fans were even spinning! Not until I had my ear 6" from the case could I hear anything. Fantastic.

I swapped my top exhaust fan for a NF-F12, which is also pretty quiet, but I wish I had spent the extra $10 for another A12. This is not only because the A12's are even quieter, but their minimum PWM setting seems to be closer to 20% and I can't seem to control the F12's with less than 36%. For me this is fine because at anything below 50%, the F12 is also basically inaudible. However, if I was trying to truly build a ZERO noise box, I would want the lowest minimum duty cycle possible on the fans.

The short story is this... I am a full Noctua convert now. I will NEVER build a PC with anything but A12's--until Noctua comes out will something better! I hate the color, but love the performance. I was really considering dropping down to a Ryzen7 just because I didn't like the high idle temps I got with fans tuned down to a tolerable whine, but not anymore! Quieter rig and 8C lower idle temps? Yes please! These fans are so worth the $30 each, it sickens me.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I ordered 8 fans for my PC to switch out my old fans in my 2019 self-built, budget PC. All fans were replaced. The exhaust and intake, and for my new CPU air cooler (not noctua), the stock fans were replaced with these. After much research, the NF-F12 (pressure oriented) and NF-S12A (heavily airflow oriented/very low pressure), looked to be quite a sacrifice in performance over minimal price difference. AKA, the price:performance ratio wasn't worth it for me when it wasn't far from an A12x25 PWM.

Spending $260 for some fans was painful, I'll admit. But when the mean time to failure rate for these fans is 150,000 hours or 17.1232877 *YEARS*, and their warranty is 6 years, my investment was made
(felt) easier!

First off: Noise
Right before these fans, I had the redux fans installed (NF-P12 redux-1700 PWM) as my 3 - 120mm intake ones for about 2 weeks, before returning them for these A12x25 fans. And man, they were LOUD. Most of the games I play really heat up my PC (Flight sim, Star Citizen, Apex Legends), therefore my fans are often spinning on the upper side of their RPM range.
These A12x25 fans at high speeds can be loud, but they have a nice white noise with acoustics that sound like they were thoughtfully engineered. Honestly, anything above 1500 RPM is noticeable. Going into this brand of fans, I had expectations wayyy too high and expected them to never make a single sound. This is definitely achievable with limiting their speeds or getting fans with ultra low noise, but that starts to cost your cooling performance.

Good news though! When my PC is idling, I actually have the opposite problem where the fans are so quiet that my refrigerator hum is no longer opposed and is singlehandedly driving me crazy with its "weeerrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr".

Performance:
Genuinely noticeable. Both with temp sensor reading and especially holding my hand over the exhaust fans. Again, in my previous set up had budget Arctic fans and had an AIO cooler. Now, I have all A12x25 fans and a Thermalright Phantom Spirit 120SE heatsink. My temperatures on my CPU as well as my overall GPU temps have gone down a lot. Like by 10C or more. Even on my CPU when I used the stock cooler fans on the Thermalright vs noctua fans, noticeable difference in temperature and noise there. The performance to noise ratio is phenomenal, with some games like Minecraft, GTA V, and a couple other low power games, performing well without any fan noise!

Price:
You get what you pay for in life. And with this fan, you DEFINITELY get what you paid for. That price is an excellent representation of its worth. I just hate myself that I justified a $33 price point per fan, but I am so happy.

Quality:
Fans are heavy and feel like they were built carefully and beautifully. They come with a LARGE selection of addons included in the packaging like rubber "Screws", metal screws, pre-installed anti vibration pads around each corner, even an extra anti vibration sleeve to even further decrease vibration, a y-cable, extension cable, and low noise adapter supplies. All this included in a fancy package, with more packaging information then you could ever want to learn about with the fans.

I don't know how I feel about having so many attachments, as I only used 2 y-cable and 2 extension cords. Which leaves me with about 36 unused accessories total. Which I will obviously not throw away, but doubt I will use any more for many many years to come. So I am torn on that large surplus of accessories but at least you get more than you need, rather than needing more than you have. Having 8 fan packages open on your floor will definitely require some space, so be tidy when you open them to prevent having a large organizational mess.

Overall:
This fan came out on May 2, 2018, and has yet to be superseded by a better Noctua fan nor any other brand. I sincerely doubt that an upgraded version will be substantially better in the near future. Just like with video game graphics, they are already fantastic and it takes a lot to improve it just a little. I feel like it may be the same with aerodynamics and fans. In the end, this investment is worthwhile and will last you for possibly decades with a performance that will be unlikely exponentially bested in the fan's lifetime. Do yourself a favor and start upgrading your PC fans. Start with intake first, then exhaust. Then consider your cooling systems too, but as they have the least amount of fans that make noise, I suggest starting with your case fans first in my personal opinion.

The only regret you'll have is that you didn't buy these fans first.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
"Plug and Play" - literally for these. Maybe not "plug" so much as "take out 13 screws" after spending an hour searching for the driver, search another hour for the plastic pry tool, half an hour prying the laptop apart safely and finally removing the RAM cover.

The laptop was a hassle but, the RAM was not. Once the old RAM was removed, this went right in. I also installed a second SSD at the time.

Upon testing, it took a few reboots for the BIOS to sync up and everything worked fine.

There's been a lot of questions on these computers handling more RAM due to the manufacturer listing only 64GB. I'm not sure why they did that. I think it may have been copy/paste from old marketing documents honestly. 96GB works fine and the chipset can actually handle more if the form-factor could. I haven't even updated the BIOS BTW. This is out of the box.

Nice and fast. Memtest good. Expected speeds.

As for value, I always have a hard time deciding with things like this. I feel they're all overpriced because they can be but I suppose relatively speaking, this was worth it. It got my laptop minimally acceptable. For my work, 96GB can get used fairly quick. Time to upgrade again! lol.

Seriously though, 0 issues. I never have issues with Vengeance though. It's always worked out for me. Just make sure you're checking your form factor and speed primarily. Some boards are picky about timing.

More importantly is if you're trying to overclock. These laptops like I have that do support 6400mhz require CSODIMM or CUSODIMM (I'm not familiar), not normal SODIMM. This does not apply to this RAM. I'm leaving this for if you're browsing or thinking of trying to overclock this. If you are going to try to OC this on an Arrowlake, don't!!! At least not to my understanding! You want the new CSODIMM for DDR5. DDR6 is another story. Don't you just love RAM? Make sure you know what you're buying because it often is not returnable once opened!

Anyway, thank you seller. My laptop is now not bottlenecked.

I’ve been building PCs for a while, gaming, content creation, and sometimes even working on tight low-profile builds. Noctua fans are always a go-to for me, and the NF-A9x14 PWM is no exception.

First off, the looks: let’s be real, the classic beige-and-brown Noctua color scheme is not exactly pretty, and honestly, it never matches my cases. I’ve never had a Noctua fan die on me, and their thermal paste kits are just as good, always my go-to for builds.

Yes, Noctua fans cost a bit more than the cheap brands, but it’s worth it for the peace of mind. You get what you pay for: quiet operation, long lifespan, and consistently good airflow. The included 4-pin PWM connector means it’s compatible with basically any modern motherboard, and you get precise fan control in BIOS or with your favorite software.

For anyone who builds their own PCs, whether you’re a gamer, a content creator, or just want a reliable and quiet fan, Noctua is a name you can trust. I’m a bit of a tech junkie, and I always find myself coming back to Noctua for any important cooling job.

text:
Reviewing the Noctua NF-A9x14 PWM:
I bought two of these Noctua fans for my dual-zone solid state (non-refrigerant) wine chiller. The original fans that removed heat from the hot side of the Peltier modules (the solid state coolers) were very noisy.
After measuring them, I realized that they were a standard size and that Noctura made fans that size.
The only modification needed was drilling out the Noctura fan mounting holes to work in my wine chiller.

I had always used Noctura fans when building computers and have felt they were the best and quietest computer fans out there. So, when I needed quieter fans for a wine chiller, I knew Noctura would come through for me.
Their appearance is great for certain computer cases but not so important when they're hidden inside a wine chiller.
They provide at least as much cooling for the Peltier modules as the original fans.

In solid state wine chillers the fans tend to run almost continuously due to the relatively weak chilling ability of the Peltier modules. Keeping the air inside at 55 F when the room is 75 F can be taxing.
So, having well-functioning and quiet fans for years is a must.

Noctua fans are a top-shelf solution and are definitely not cheap compared to the bottom-tier choices.
But in the long run, not having to tear into a computer or wine chiller sooner than expected due to a fan failure is enough of a reason for me to want to pay more.
I'm a big "fan" of Noctua fans.

So, I installed a Noctua 140mm fan in the PSU (since it's out of warranty now anyway) and replaced the CPU cooler fan with this Noctua 90mm fan (a like for like replacement). In my previous setup, I was not using the low-noise connector that you get in the Noctua box. However, this time I installed the low-noise connector on both the CPU fan and the PSU fan, and connected both fans directly to the Motherboard for optimum fan performance and monitoring.

Without the low-noise connectors, the system was extremely quiet and never intruded on my movies or TV shows. And now with the low-noise connectors installed, the system is so quiet you cannot hear it at all! I also have a passively cooled nVidia GT1030 graphics card in the case, creating additional heat and have not noticed any problems or noise increase.

Quiet - With the low-noise connector, I have to shine a flashlight into the case to see if the fans are spinning! >.<

Effective - My tiny mini-ITX case remains cool and operational even after hours of use.

Reliable - After almost 7 years of daily use, it's still going strong! Why did I replace it then? Simply for peace of mind.

From a sheer performance perspective, and I'm talking pushing the most air through your case or into a heatsink, and doing so quietly, these fans are tough to beat. Considering they're only 15mm thick, I put them into my own best-of-class category.

But while they do work great, they are on the flimsy side. I'll give you an example. After looking up the stats and reading some reviews, I decided to replace a competitor fan (name begins with 'Noc') with the P12 Slim in a sub-5 liter mini-itx case.

I found the P12 to have slightly better performance by 2-3 degrees C in my case overall, with the noise the same as the Noc, at less than half the price. Only, when I first closed the case, the P12 wobbled at slow speeds, making an obvious noise along with it at startup and shutdown. This lasted for about 3 startups/shutdowns and just went away. I checked cables and all were clear, so it had to be coming from the fan. Considering its the same size as the other fan, which had no weird noise issues, I just felt the word flimsy came to mind. Maybe it twisted slightly to fit or something? I couldn't tell by looking. I'm not going to take a star off for this, but just be aware. I would have returned it if things didn't settle down.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I did a review on a set of these before. I may have been a little hard on Fasgear. These three power supply 8 pin cables to one PCIe5 12v connector do work fine for my RTX 4080. The plugs seem to be of good quality, and the wirers are sufficient to carry the load. The wirers in the harness are individually shieled, but the harness is not sleeved as the description may lead you to believe. I had to tape mine every 5 inches to make a neat cable.

They are a mix of black and white wirers, so it doesn't look awful, but Fasgear should have bundled the wirers from where they merge with the three 8 pin leads to the 12v 16 pin connector. They are hard wirers, so they don't bend easily, but as long as the edge of your GPU is at least 1 to 1-1/4 inches from the side of your case, you will be able to bend them enough, so they don't rub on the side of your case.

Make sure that you order the cables for your PSU so that you will get the right connectors for the 8 pin plugs. If you don't have three 8 pin connectors free on your PSU, then you probably need to upgrade your PSU. If this is the case then you should probably ne looking for a PCIe5 PSU as you then will have a 16 pin 12 volt connector and then you just need the single 16 pin to 16 pin cable, which will carry the voltage evenly from the PSU to your GPU.

Even though the 8 pin connectors on a PSU are rated for 150 volts, the PSU will deliver what ever the GPU calls for up to whatever it's max output is, but the possible fly in the ointment is that the PSU will not output the same wattage at each connector, so although any good PSU will put out more than the recommended 150 watts from any one connector, you may end up with a large enough disparity between the wattage output on the three 8 pin connectors to cause enough voltage variation at the 16 pin connector, which may cause unexpected shut downs due to safeguards in either the GPU or the PSU.

With all that said, the gauge of the wirers in the harness is sufficient to handle the maximum 600 watts that the GPU could theoretically draw, but it would be a rare case for a 4080 to ask for more than 350 watts. Anyway, I haven't had any issues that I would attribute to power draw from the GPU using this Fasgear harness so far, and I really don't think a 4070Ti or the 4080 will have any problems with this setup.

text:
Corsairs 2.5" to 3.5" HDD mount was almost perfection for upgrading my parent's 2007 Core 2 Duo iMac 7,1 (24") from a 3.5" 360GB 7200RPM HDD to a 240GB PNY SSD.

What made this bracket better than the others for this upgrade is that the 2.5" mount is placed at the top of the bracket instead of the center. This is great because in the 7,1 series of iMacs, the Sata power and data cables are very short and just barely reach the factory 3.5" standard HDD and wouldn't be able to be connected to a center mounted converter bracket.

When you install this bracket in a 7,1 iMac, it's installed bottom (screw) side up, which means the Sata power and data cable of the 2.5" drive are on the bottom and the 2.5" drive is upside down. (Label side of drive facing towards the back of the iMac)

The only problem is that the mounting bracket is a little short. (As other have said) - This was okay for me, because the mount is attached with a peg and clamp for installation in the iMac. Only one (out of two) of the pegs could not be attached, but one was enough and SSDs can't be damaged if it vibrates or moves.

I'm using these with Nvidia RTX 3090 GPUs and they are working fine.

The PCIe outputs are functionally the same, even though the pins come from different wires than the Corsair HX1500i cables.

I used a multimeter and continuity testing to verify, as I didn't want to fry a 3090. Here's the diagram, showing the ground ("G") and +12V pins for both the Corsair and Certusfun cables. Even though they come from different wires, the pinout achieves the same ground and +12V on all the same output pins.

Cable thickness is good (looks like 14GA, and not the 16GA of some other cables) and same size as the original Corsair cables. I have no doubt they would deliver adequate current to the GPUs.

Listing description specifically states this cable is compatible with my Corsair RM 750X. The list of incompatible devices on the description gives no indication this cable would be incompatible with my PSU.

In theory, you could take a slim hot knife and create the gap where it is needed.

1. You will no longer be able to return the item.

The cable sent is also not missing a metal piece in one of the little squares like in the OEM plugs. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I ordered this because I had a defective Arctic Liquid Freezer III 240mm AIO. I don't return broken products. I let the company keep the money so they can maybe one day fix their stupidity.... on that note I wont continue to complain about the Arctic Cooler!

This unit was extremely simple to install. One thing I noticed in terms of design was that you rotate the cooler 90 degrees for AMD where the tubes are either left/right of the CPU socket where as Intel will have the tubes top/bottom. Wont knock a star for aesthetics, I bought something that needs to cool my PC and its doing it swimmingly (ha, water joke).

I skipped out on using the MSI paste. I never trust paste that comes with manufacturer parts. Not knocking MSI, the paste is probably decent. But I want the highest quality paste possible. KINGPIN KPx is known to be insane especially for overclocking, which means it will remain cool. I usually buy Arctic Silver 5 (different "arctic" company than the AIO company) but lately on Amazon they are sold by 3rd party and shipped by Amazon. For all I know those pastes have been sitting for so long they "separated" by now. Not gonna risk it. The KPx I got was sold and shipped my Amazon. Hashtag winning (haha). So far my temps have been great and there is no weird noises. Double winning. I have my fans in push pull as per image. With rear fan as exhaust and PSU as exhaust. I know weird right? Most people would want their PSU to get fresh air.... WELL, this improves airflow so that air moves bottom to top of case. It works.

Many will notice the slim fans at the bottom. This is a jonsbo d32pro case. And you can also notice the motherboard is a back connect b650m project zero board. All connectors are on the back! making it super sleek and once again improving airflow. So if you are curious if you can fit the 7900xtx Red Devil from PowerColor utilizing this motherboard (top slot is x16 as apposed to many m-atx boards where its second slot) then you CAN fit two slim fans down there. I think I could have wedged in some full size fans, but I like having the air gap to help with any turbulence that might occur between the two. So far my temps are insanely low. But that's to be expected since all sides of the case are perforated except for the glass side cover that is frosted black (not installed in picture).

Obviously I didn't use the MSI fans... I dont care for RGB. And sure enough the only light from my pc comes from the GPU which is always red because "designed that way." I could plug in some color matching cables into the gpu but im lazy and that's also extra cables on the front section which I dont want. I like it clean.... So I cant comment on fan brightness/quality, or even the AIO pump section lighting. Its all disabled.

Value for money? I mean its a 240mm AIO and its not the cheapest but also not the most expensive. Its working. I dont have hard testing data to say if its good or not, maybe one of the youtuber reviewers will get to this unit eventually.... for now, its working, and that's all that matters.

The tubes are VERY easy to move around, which I like. The Arctic tubes are so hard to bend that manhandling them makes you cringe. These, they have a bit of flop but retain some stiffness. IMO the perfect "in-between."

SADLY, I ruined my silver/black aesthetic I was originally going for. I already own like 12 noctua NF-A12x25 fans so reusing them after having to rebuild my system after a failed Arctic AIO, I said EFF it. Performance is more important. No, I am not spending $100's of dollars to buy all the fans I have in black flavor.... waste of money when I have perfectly functional fans I can use. And this is only 5 of them. I have more in storage.... This build was a consolidation of size. I wanted something smaller and sleeker. I had a huge case that was super large prior which had all the fans installed including push/pull on a 360mm aio. But 360mm aio on a 7800x3d is overkill, so far my temps look the same as my 360mm setup previously. So winning.

text:
Despite being relatively tech-savvy, this motherboard was used in the first PC I built from scratch. During that process, I learned three things everyone should know.

1) If you put an AMD Ryzen 5 or newer processor (mine was originally the 5500 and I swapped it to the 5500 GT), then you need to flash the BIOS. Even if you did everything correctly, you could still be missing monitor output. As scary as it sounds because people have bricked their MOBO before, flashing the BIOS isn't especially difficult. All you need is a spare 8GB Flashdrive that you can reformat. I won't go through the full list of instructions, but there are plenty of tutorials out there.

2) This is an optional step, but I /highly/ recommend getting a CPU with integrated graphics (remember, I swapped from the 5500 to the 5500 GT). It costs a little more money, but it can make the initial Windows install and driver updates infinitely easier. If the BIOS is flashed, then the CPU should work. If the CPU works, and you have integrated graphics, then you can do the entire setup process and have a much easier time troubleshooting any GPU problems you could encounter.

3) I ran into very, very weird compatibility issues with one of the off-brand RX 580s you can find on Amazon (hence recommending integrated graphics for troubleshooting). The GPU worked, but it only worked when I slotted it into my PC I've had since 2019. It never worked on this motherboard. I slotted a random, old GPU I had sitting around (9500 GT), and it DID work on this motherboard. Despite using the other GPU to install Windows and drivers, I could never get any display output using that RX 580. That said, I wouldn't blame the motherboard for issues with an off-brand component originally manufactured 7 years ago. Ended up shelling out an extra $60 to get an RTX 3050 just to get something from a reputable company.

Your mileage may vary with this motherboard, but so long as you have integrated graphics, buy a reputable GPU, and are willing to learn how to flash the BIOS (which isn't bad at all on this motherboard), then you'll probably get an amazing value.

text:
I wanted a new laptop for personal use as well as mostly moderate gaming, and this laptop is great for all my purposes (i9, 32GB RAM, 1TB storage). I consider the price I paid ($1746) reasonable compared with similar laptops, but it does go on sale sometimes.

The laptop is a little on the heavy and slightly bulky side for casual use, but I wouldn’t have minded if it was even bigger than it is if that meant better cooling, less cost, etc. It really not too bulky for a gaming laptop. Size aside, it looks great. Stylish and sleek, and the customizable and dimmable keyboard backlighting is a nice touch. I like the keyboard layout for typing as well as gaming, I find it to be very functional. The number pad is small but usable. The function keys are well thought out (function keys for screen brightness, keyboard backlighting brightness, enable/disable touchpad, mute mic, etc.), which I find to be rare with laptops. There’s a light for function lock and mic muting. WASD are a different color for gaming.

The laptop runs Windows 11 well and seems very fast and powerful (although I haven’t done anything yet to truly push its limits). The BIOS is pretty reasonable, based on my experience (IT professional). The MSI app with designated function key lets you quickly change the power mode for your purposes, although my limited experience with the AI mode has not been great so far (it throttled the power down when I needed it, reasons unknown, and it turned off the keyboard backlighting at night). I’ve only played a few games on it so far, but it handles Fortnite like a champ without needing its full capabilities (power setting on “balanced” works perfectly). I haven’t run into any major issues with other programs or OS yet. Worth noting, the laptop does not always shut down properly. I’ve had to disable sleep and hibernation in Windows, as the laptop frequently does not resume from those states gracefully. Sometimes the laptop does not shut down completely at all, and the Embedded Controller keeps the fans running indefinitely, until I hold down the power button to manually power it off. That’s not ideal, but for me it’s not too big a deal either.

The laptop also runs hot when in performance power mode or when gaming. I would never use a gaming laptop without a cooling pad, but if you’re new to gaming laptops, take note. The laptop seems to manage its built in fans well (and there’s a keyboard function key to let you immediately turn all the fans on to max speed), but again, I advise a cooling pad with fans to ensure you don’t overheat it during any use more intensive than watching videos. Definitely don’t ever put this down on a soft surface (like a bed or couch) without a hard flat surface under it or you’ll probably melt it.

The power supply is bulky, as you would expect for a laptop that needs extra power for gaming, and the power supply also gets hot. Best to keep it where it can easily cool when in use. The power cord has a third prong/ground.

All around, a great gaming laptop for a reasonable price.

Moved my last build into a new case, replaced my huge air cooler with the MAG CORELIQUID A15 240.

This is my first experience using liquid cooling. I had the biggest baddest air cooler and wasn't real happy with it's performance in my 14900k build. Figured I'd give this cooler a shot, I was moving into a new case anyway.

The install was easy, not any more difficult than installing any other cooler. I was pleasantly surprised when I first fired up the rebuild, my temps were down considerably compared to my air cooler with the 240 cooler installed in the top panel. The fans that come with the cooler aren't bad, they're quiet, push a decent amount of air and don't require a fan header that pulls over 1amp.
If you're going to do a push pull configuration you'll need to get extra fan screws separately. The kit does not include extra fans screws, only the screws on the pre installed fans. There are plenty of case screws.

The 360 A15 will be my next liquid cooler for a new build. I can only imagine how the 360 A15 will perform when the 240's performance was so impressive right out of the box.

text:
Purchased this PSU as a first step effort to repair a freezing new PC build that was leaning on an older, excellent EVGA PSU that was well past its own 10 year warranty. While the EVGA PSU was ultimately not to blame, I did keep this MSI one on hand to keep vendor variety to a minimum on my MSI 870 Tomahawk build that was still giving me issues, and it was nice to have a power supply that natively had the 12VHPWR cabling available.

I appreciate the modular design of this PSU, the only variety I tend to buy these days, and this one in particular has a much smaller footprint than the one it ended up replacing which affords more room during the cramped cabling stage. I do find it much more difficult to remove the cables from this PSU than I do others that I own, something that can be a bit of a pain when you're trying to remove just a single cable rather than the whole PSU to do so. While the warranty is amazing in length (10 years!), I can say from having to deal with MSI's warranty service for the motherboard, I'm not a huge fan of the process; primarily they're quite slow to turn things around, and will use the slowest shipping process available (not to mention shipping to them on your dime). There's also no Advanced RMA option (though that seems to be losing favor in general with companies). Contrast that with other vendors like AMD who sprung for overnight inbound shipping for me and used 2 day to send parts back and I'm hoping I don't need to lean on them for this PSU in the future.

Overall though, I'm happy to have this more condensed unit in my new build and it shows no signs of trouble with my limited use case thus far.

3 Months Later: Fan already seems to be failing a bit; PSU still works fine, but the thing is easily the loudest component in my PC while idling...in a case where there are at least 10 other fans to compete with. A bit disappointed with it, though probably not worth a warranty replacement yet, assuming MSI would humor one at all for mere fan noise. Worth shaving a star off; this one pales in comparison to the now ancient EVGA PSU it replaced.

text:
This review is for the 240mm MAG AIO. I got this to pair with my MSI Z690I Unity motherboard, everything is mounted in a Lian Li Dan H20 case (small ITX case designed with a 240mm AIO in mind)

The good:
- It's got great thermo performance. At full load (12700k) I am not breaking 70C. As I am writing this the CPU package is barely above room temperature
- It's quiet, even when gaming at full blast you can barely hear the fan. In fact if you have an air cooled GPU, the GPU probably makes more noise at full blast than the fans. BUT... (more below)

The bad:
- The mounting holes for the screws were not very well stamped or drilled. I find screwing in the radiator to the case mounting brackets to be somewhat difficult - the provided holes seems just a tat too small for the screws and some of the mounting points "fins" were not stamped / bend in such a way that wasn't flushed. I find myself having to take a needle nose pliers to adjust a couple of the tabs to make the mounting works
- The pump noise... not noticeable when everything is at full blast but when everything is quiet (like just browsing the web) that high pitch background whine from the water pump is quite noticeable and annoying.
- Tight fitment for ITX builds... Like most other CPU AIO on the market, the tubes are feeding the CPU waterblock comes out on the side. This is a very tight fit on high end ITX motherboards. Expecially those with very tall integrated m.2 heatsink blocking the bottom. This one fits but the tubes were pretty much right up against the RAM. A top feed waterblock design like the Artic Freezer might work better for tight ITX builds.

text:
Dopo aver provato diversi dissipatori, l'MSI MPG CORELIQUID P13 360 si distingue immediatamente per un motivo: la pulizia visiva. È il componente perfetto per chi cerca una build ordinata e futuristica.

Display LCD da 2.1" e Modalità "Extended Display":
Il pezzo forte è il display IPS circolare protetto da un vetro curvo che sembra una goccia d'acqua. Tramite MSI Center, oltre a monitorare temperature e frequenze, ho potuto sfruttare la funzione Extended Display: lo schermo viene visto dal PC come un monitor secondario, permettendo di trascinare piccoli widget o animazioni personalizzate con una fluidità incredibile.

Design Streamline: Addio cavi a vista
La cosa che più mi ha entusiasmato è la gestione dei cavi. MSI ha integrato tutto all'interno dei tubi: non ci sono cavi che escono dal blocco della pompa. Questo, unito alle ventole CycloBlade 9 pre-installate sul radiatore, riduce drasticamente il tempo di montaggio e rende l'interno del case estremamente pulito, ideale per chi usa case con vetro temperato.

Prestazioni e Silenziosità:
Non è solo bello: la base in rame senza viti e i micro-canali ottimizzati tengono a bada anche le CPU più calde (come i nuovi Intel Core Ultra). Le ventole sono sorprendentemente silenziose anche sotto carico, e la pompa da 3400 RPM fa un lavoro eccellente senza produrre ronzii fastidiosi.

Se cercate un dissipatore che unisca prestazioni termiche di alto livello a un'estetica mozzafiato, il P13 360 è la scelta obbligata. Trasforma letteralmente l'aspetto del PC.

Conclusión: Es una placa base robusta, con gran conectividad WiFi y un diseño sólido. Si ya tienes tornillería de repuesto, es una compra totalmente recomendada, pero ten en cuenta que el kit de accesorios es bastante básico.

text:
Le MSI MAG CORELIQUID E240 est mon tout premier kit de watercooling, et honnêtement, je craignais un peu l’installation. Finalement, tout s’est très bien passé : une fois que l’on comprend la logique, le montage est vraiment simple et fluide. Les pièces s’assemblent bien, tout est bien conçu et on sent la qualité MSI.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
At $300, this was the most expensive motherboard I have purchased by a long shot, but my timing was very fortunate as there was a $60 off coupon that brought the price down to $240. There is a very noticeable difference in terms of the weight and rigidity of this board compared to the cheaper boards I have purchased in the past, and that just feels like quality to me. MSI stresses the easiness of installation with this board, and they did implement a few nifty features that are actually worthy improvements. The first is the tool-less NVME SSD Frozr Shields and spring clips that don’t require screws to hold the drives in place. The other, which I totally missed when doing my build, is the EZ Front Panel Cable that is really like an extension cable, but I can definitely see where it facilitates the process of connecting tiny plugs onto tiny pins. Something this board does that no other board I have owned does is that it pauses for a couple of “Mississippi’s” during boot up at the screen where you would tap on Delete to enter bios. This screen usually just blinks and immediately vanishes, which is why we are all in the habit of spamming the Delete button as soon as the boot up starts, but I have been able to get into bios with just a single press of Delete because of this pause. No flashy design and no RGB, just a solid, well-built board with all the features I would ever want or need. And it does come with the Reduced Load ILM (RL-ILM) that is supposed to eliminate the bending issue from the previous generation of CPUs on the LGA 1700 socket.

There are 2 things I want to note: the first being that an NVME drive installed in slot 01 will get pretty hot when gaming because it’s right under the GPU. My NVME increased 10C with just moderate gaming, so it’s better to use slots 03 or 04. The 2nd thing is that Amazon defaulted to shipping this motherboard in the factory box and it (the box) arrived with the flap open and a few dings in it. Fortunately, the board was okay, but the factory box is for store display and not shipping. Make sure to select “ship in Amazon packaging” to get proper protection.

The motherboard is equipped with x2 M.2 slots (with one optional heatsink), x6 SATA ports, customisable RGB lights on the board itself (as shown in their product picture), x3 PCIe slots, a dedicated RGB LED connector, an easy to utilise overclocking feature within the BIOS, and 6 fan slots overall (2 PWM's and 4 DC's). There are many more options, but way too many to list. This motherboard has everything required for a solid gaming, desktop, or workstation build. I currently have mine paired with a EVGA 1070 Ti, a Samsung 970 EVO 500GB M.2 (as boot drive), a WD Blue 500GB M.2, G.SKILL Ripjaws 2400 (2x8GB), Corsair TX750M 80+ GOLD, and an Intel i5-9600K.

The user interface is very friendly and the BIOS is easy to navigate. The board itself is very easy to install and comes with clear instructions on where everything goes. If you're not sure on how to install one of the cables based off of the manual, then MSI does offer QR codes that link to YouTube videos for more visual-oriented folks.

I do dislike the Mystic Light program, however, as it doesn't play well with my other RGB control applications (in particular, my G.SKILL KM780 RBG Keyboard's program). It automatically syncs my keyboard to motherboard without option for my keyboard to "wave" through the other colours (it keeps it at a solid red and flickers/spazzes out when I attempt to change my keyboard back to previous settings). If you're looking for a solid motherboard with some nice RGB features, then this is the board for you. It does have its small problems (application wise) but, otherwise, MSI continues to impress with their products.I am absolutely in love with their motherboards.

BIOS is extremely easy to use and with F7 will switch between easy mode or advanced mode. One click overclocking for CPU and RAM, AMD SAM was already enabled and ready to go. No bloatware except a single bottom corner Norton security pop up when powering on the system each time but I believe that is from MSI Afterburner software if you refuse it when downloading. Otherwise just don't get MSI Afterburner and you won't get the pop up. Norton security is nowhere else to be found thankfully.

WIFI does not work when first time booting, must use Ethernet cable, and download wifi driver later. Of which the antenna works really well and 16 feet from my router through two walls I am only seeing a 60mbs drop in speed, getting 240 out of 300mb/s.

This thing is quite large so do be sure to check your case dimensions.

Comes with NVME thermal plates with built in pads on top and bottom of NVME and the bottom plate cannot be removed so third party NVME heat sink cannot be used. But with this built in top and bottom I don't see the need for additional cooling as what's there seems to be sufficient. However if you get a thicker NVME with a built in heatsink/graphene strip, at just 4mm it's nearly too thick to mount it between both thermal pads with heat sink plates. They really need to fix this on this board but not a deal breaker....unless you got a thick NVME of course like a SAMSUNG EVO or BLACK. My HP 4TB NVME has a graphene thermal tape strip on it and it was difficult to sandwich in there.

Overall highly pleased, board is overbuilt making it solid, cool running, and you don't have to worry about pulling too much power or power limitations.

Some key reminders for your build:
* This motherboard requires DDR5 RAM. I actually realized this too late and had to throw out my old DDR4 RAM… good thing it’s cheap enough that I didn’t mind this upgrade.
* If you are loading in a pre-existing hard drive/SSD: before you disassemble your old rig, make sure you are “UEFI ready”!! I was upgrading from a 9 year old motherboard, so my SSD was still configured for MBR (master boot record) which is old-school BIOS friendly. This MSI motherboard requires the new UEFI system, so you need to convert an old hard drive to be UEFI-ready (GPT = GUID Partition Table). This is really simple/fast with a Windows provided exe called MBR2GPT, there are guides online that show you how to do this on the command line. I did NOT know this before, so I had to reassemble my old rig just to run this step, which formatted my SSD to the correct partition style for UEFI. Then, my new MSI booted up automatically to Windows.

We had an old laptop that died recently and wouldn't be worth repairing, so while the October Prime Days event was on I looked for something that should be somewhat 'future proof' with good specs at a price less than $1000. I picked the MSI Katana A15 AI 15.6” 144Hz FHD Gaming Laptop with the Ryzen 7-9945HS and NVIDIA Geforce RTX 4060, 32Gb RAM, and 1TB SSD.
It was on sale for $879 plus tax at the time, which was a really good price for the specs.
It has all the ports we need for plugging in different devices, the keyboard feels good, and the screen is bright & crisp with a 144Hz refresh rate that keeps up with the busiest action scenes in games and movies. The screen is a bit more 'letter box' shape than I'd really like, but that's the only thing I can find to whine about. It's a bit heavy compared to some, but that isn't an issue for us.
It runs all our small business office and accounting software silently, without the cooling system kicking in at all. The only time it cools itself is when playing graphic intensive games, and IMHO the fan noise isn't bad at all. Most of the time it sits on a multi fan cooling pad, but even without that turned on the laptop never gets particularly hot.
All in all, it was a great deal, so if it's on sale for less than $900 again, snap it up. Even at around $1050 I think it's still a worthy contender.
