It would have been great, if it hadn’t come with manufacturing defects. I took a chance on an open box unit for sale during Prime day. The significant discount brought the cost down to about the price of the Thermalright Aqua Elite 120 AIO, so I thought why not take the gamble. Boy was I wrong! Long story short was that the CoolerMaster product had a manufacturing defect out of the box. Luckily I discovered this when trying to mount the included fan onto the radiator, before I went through the trouble of removing my air cooler and adjusting my case for the AIO’s placement. From the pictures, you can see that only one fan screw can go in on any side, which subsequently would cause the other holes on all adjacent sides to be out of alignment. text:
I have come to really trust Thermalright brand. This is my third Thermalright product and all of them have performed really well, and the prices are substantially lower than comparable competitions.

This AIO was packaged well in a fairly large box. Everything was well organized, and installation was fairly straightforward. Construction of the unit itself is top notch. While someone may not like the appearance of the pump on the hosts, I actually really like the fact that the pump is not on top of the CPU; the hosts can dampen any vibration coming from the pump. A minor issue is the fact that the cables for the fans are all loose and not bundle together. But they can all be hidden below the MB and out of sight.

If you have a hot running CPU like 13th or 14th generation i7 (I have i7 13700K), this AIO can really tame the temperature. Idle temperature is mid 20's C while upper 50's to lower 60's under load (Topaz AI, LrC, and Photoshop). Temperature can spike to mid 80's for a second or so and then drop down to 70's when cooling catches up. I am sure some tuning of the fan and CPU parameters can further minimize the spike, but it does not bother me at all.

This AIO has eliminated my concern regarding potential thermal damage of the CPU. There is always the potential of leakage especially down the road, but I cannot comment on that at this point.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I have been using and testing this AIO since I received it shortly after Black Friday. Please note that my computer sits on a separate platform next to my computer, so it's about 2.5 feet away from my ears, and it's contained in a Corsair 5000x RGB. Intel 12700k CPU, Asus TG H670 Pro Wifi D4 mobo.

I ran this in all 3 positions (top, side, front), with tubes up and down (front & side).

Even during Cinebench, LinPack Extreme, Time Spy and Prime 95, the temperatures ranged no higher than 89C with ambient (room) temperature around 23C. It was always quiet although, after the few 3 months, I noticed an occasional harmonic resonance tone, which I assume was from the fans, and I little bit of noise from the pump. The best position for both the CPU and GPU in my case was on the side, exhausting the air, with the tubes going from the side of the block to the top of the radiator. Indeed, it was also one of the best positions overall, as it also did a good job keeping both the VRM heatsinks and motherboard cooler than 6 of the 10 positions I have tested so far.

This is the first AIO I have tested, and you can watch my initial video about it on YT on my channel, The PC Expert Amateur. There will be at least one follow-up video with technical results once I complete the other 10 tests I need to do.

Please note that WelshyTech (YouTube) deemed this and the Frozen Magic Scenic V2 to be loud, but he has his computer on his desk less than a foot from his head. He also noted that the MS V2 is slightly more powerful than the Notte.

The mounting system is a bit awkward. At one point, I had to reorient the block and was unable to see (that's the bad thing about putting it on the floor) that I had missed putting two of the mounting screws through the bottom holes for the block, which resulted in bending them and slightly damaging the blue plastic stand-offs. Also, the knurled nuts are easy to turn by hand, and also have a large Philips cross for a screwdriver, but it is very easy to have them drop down to the bottom of the case. Aside from that, it's not bad, especially considering that you can mount the block in any orientation (I suggest top or right side). If you have a LONG graphics card and want to mount it on the front or side, you will likely have to vertically mount the GC (and if the case design is poor, as the 5000x's is, you will struggle to find a mount that won't choke the fans because it's too close to the left side panel) in order to do so. If you want to do a front mount with the tubes going to the bottom of the radiator (i.e. the radiator is positioned so that the tube apertures are at the bottom, not the top), it will probably be a tight fit, especially if you have a very long case, you may not be able to do it without modifying the tubes, so make sure that the block is mounted with the tubes on the side. Before finalizing the mounting of the block and rad, make sure to verify it will fit without putting too much pressure on the fittings on the block and rad. The block does have swiveling fittings for the tubes, so that does help, but it can still be a bit difficult.

text:
Picked up the Thermalright FW360 Black ARGB for a new AM5 build with a Ryzen 9 9950x3d. I was originally considering more well-known brands, but after seeing the price and a few online reviews, I gave this one a shot.

Installation was straightforward. Mounting hardware feels solid, and the instructions were decent, though not super detailed (if you’re new to PC building, you might want to look up a quick YouTube video). The tubing is flexible, and everything feels more premium than I expected at this price point.

Cooling performance is impressive — under full load (Cinebench and long gaming sessions), my CPU stays in the low 70s°C, and idle temps sit around 45°C. For a 360mm AIO in this price range, that’s more than acceptable.

Fans are quiet under normal loads and only ramp up under stress, but even then, noise levels are manageable. The ARGB lighting is bright and smooth. It adds a nice touch to the build without being too flashy.

Only real downside is cable clutter — with three fans and ARGB connections, it took some extra effort to keep everything neat. I had to rotate the fans from their original position to hide the cords. Also, no dedicated software. you’ll rely on motherboard control for lighting, which may or may not matter depending on your setup.

Pros:
• Excellent cooling performance for the price.
• Quiet fans under normal use.
• Good build quality, sleek all-black design.
• ARGB looks great and syncs well with MSI mobo software
• Supports current AMD socket (including AMD nextGen)

Cons:
• Cable management can be tricky (lots of connectors)
• No bundled software (all lighting/fan control via motherboard)

Bottom Line:
If you’re looking for a 360mm AIO that delivers solid thermal performance and ARGB flair without breaking the bank, the Thermalright FW360 Black ARGB is a great option. Definitely punches above its weight for the price.

text:
A friend pointed this to me when I purchased the i9-12900k in Oct 2023. I was having issues where the CPU was reaching high temps and pegging out close to 100 C and thermal throttling. I did not know that the ILM (CPU bracing bracket) on the newer chipsets tends to warp and cause the cooler not to sit properly on the CPU and keep it cooled. Once my order arrived I removed the factory ILM bracket and replaced it with this device. My water cooler now sits perfectly upon the CPU and hasn't caused any issues with cooling on my device. Max temps I have seen are around 80 C max depending on what I am working on. Even running programs such as Aida64 and stressing the CPU temps have dropped from the 100 C range down to 85 C range. This has definitely saved me from causing damage to my CPU due to heating issues. It is simple to install by simply removing the original bracket off the motherboard and utilizing the 4 screws from the original device and placing the CPU in place with thermal paste and simply mounting the bracket over the top of it and screwing it down and installing the cooler.

My wife upgraded her PC in June and went with a 12th gen i5 LGA 1700. I didn't even bother trying to install the CPU until I ordered this device and had it in hand. I didn't want to have to remove and reinstall everything like I did on mine so I waited and installed this device to be safe from the start.

text:
I purchased the Thermalright Stream Vision 360 aio for my midrange white build. The aio is brand new and not much information can be found on it at the moment. Thermalright is a reputable company with competitive pricing on their coolers so I decided to roll the dice on it.

The aio is packaged well and appears as shown. The cooler seems solidly built and installation was easy. The screen can be removed while installing for easier access and is secured to the unit via magnets. I installed this on a AMD 9800x3d cpu.

So far, I have ran this through several stress tests and extended gaming sessions and very satisfied with the performance/results. This aio keeps the 9800x3d cool with no concerns of overheating. At idle, the cpu is sitting around 30*C with my environment at approximately 21*C. The highest temps observed were mid to upper 60s during stress tests, and under 60s for multi-hour gaming sessions. Im a bit weary of the pump location being right at the hose connections, but that decision will take more time to determine the result. The aio is also abit on the louder side, but some of this can be toned down altering the fan speed curves.

The screen is crisp and the program used for customization is easy to use and surprisingly full of both pre-installed and customizable options. The fan built into the head does work at diffusing some heat away from the cpu and motherboard.

So far, I have been very happy with price to ascetic/performance and would recommend this aio. For the price, its hard to find competition offering the build quality and a screen.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I have an ASUS G15CE that came with the ROG STRIX B560-G GAMING WIFI and Intel Core i7-11700F.
Along with that, I have upgraded the RAM to Corsair LPX.
This combination is commonly known to only support 92MM air coolers.
When I got the computer, I settled for a Noctua NH-U9S Chromax as it was the best option at the time.
It got loud and it thermal throttled the CPU, limiting boost speeds.
When I saw this, I leapt at the chance to upgrade.

The Good:
It is cooler, quieter, lets my CPU run as designed, and I mean... what other metrics for evaluating a cooler are there? It's great! ... once you can get it installed.
The Bad:
For perspective: this is probably my 10th (?) cooler upgrade over the years: Arctic Cooling 64 Pro, Corsair H100i, AresGames River 5, AMD/Cooler Master Wraith to Wraith Prism (then moving that between my 1700, 3700X and 5900X...), a DeepCool AK620 CPU Air Cooler, and a Thermalright Aqua Elite 240 V3 I just got the other day. I'm sure there are a few others as well.

This is, I would say by far, the most difficult install I've done. The instructions come on a tiny strip of paper with few words and nondescript pictures. The pictures are taken from a strange 3/4 perspective with the RAM in the... bottom left of the picture at an angle rather than to the right of the CPU socket.
All installs are shown only in a small, 6-picture diagram. The process "Install the clips to the far-side of the fan with the hub facing the back of the computer, gently pull the retention clip around the fins." is explained "clip on fan".
A bag containing general parts is attached to a the AM4/AM5 bag and is unlabeled, leading one to believe all of the parts in said bag are for that install.
The screws to get the heatsink attached to the retention mechanism are maddening. They keep popping out and it takes far longer than would be necessary with decent screws.
For comparison, the Noctua NH-U9S this is replacing has three individual pamphlets with foldout and is 6 total written pages, probably... 20x the documentation. (And the Noctua is much easier to install... go figure.

Anyway, it's on there. It's working. My CPU hums along with full boost. It's quiet. It's half the price of the Noctua.

But, before buying this, you need to make sure that it's right for you. Why get this if a normal 120MM cooler would fit? They're cheaper, even better at cooling, easier to install, and would be the superior choice for the vast majority of people not building in a case with limited clearance.

Oh, and word of warning: the fan sits about 2mm proud of the heatsink. Make sure you add that to the stated dimensions: L125 mm x W110 mm x H135 mm.

The stock fan has some totally proprietary hole dimensions , unlike the A12x25r that at least has some 92 fan hole spacing on one side. I was unable to adapt a a12x25r onto this cooler.

Compared to NH-D12L that I also have, it has similar performance in terms of wattage it can cool. The TR may even be better but I did not perform a controlled test. The D12L is on a different CPU with different paste. But overall the performance-value is great, even if you may decide to get some aftermarket fans for this cooler.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought 3 of the Thermalright AssassinX120 R SE ARGB CPU Air Coolers.

2 for new computer builds and 1 to replace a Deep Cool basic CPU cooler in a prebuilt. The first 2 coolers keep the CPU around 60C during a stress test. Keeping an AMD Ryzen 5600X and a Ryzen 5600G running at about 60C at max.

My 5600G came out of and HP Victus and then installed in an ASUS B450 motherboard. I needed a new cooler, and this one was priced right and had ARGB. Perfect to link up with my other fans. The 5600G under stress testing stayed within 63-65C .

The 5600X originally had the stock AMD cooler when built and was running up to 85C. I bought this cooler again and it brought temperature down 20C or more under stress testing.

My original pre-build was upgraded from a Ryzen 3100 to a 5600X. The basic Deep Cool cooler let the CPU get to 83C and a bit higher under stress testing. I bought the Thermalright cooler for a 3rd time knowing that it would cool the CPU much better. However, the 3rd cooler had an issue. When installing the cooler onto the brackets, one side would not screw down correctly. The resulted in the cooler not being in contact with the CPU correctly and the thermal paste not being distributed correctly. The CPU temperature ran hotter than the original cooler even at idle. I requested a replacement, and I am happy to say the replacement works as intended. The photos are CPU temperature and Clock speeds while stress testing with the Deel Cool running 83C and then the Thermalright running 20C+ cooler. CPU clock speeds between the two coolers is closer to the max with the Thermalright

Although the 3rd cooler was defective, the fast replacement more than makes up for the issue.

The thermal paste that comes with the unit is good for one CPU. It does work and is what I used on the CPUs. However, it does get very tacky when cold and another better paste is recommended. I had issues getting the cooler off the CPU. Did not have issues with a better paste in the past.

Nice cooler for the price and really does cool the CPU a good 20C under load vs stock.

Excellent cooler by ThermalRight!

Keeping my Ryzen 5 9600X nice and cool - allows PBO AUTO mode have a steady average CPU clock of 5,425MHz and an average temperature of 60 degrees Celsius while gaming. Sweet! Along with my 9070 XT and 32GB of DDR 5 6000 makes for a perfect cool gaming PC on a budget. Love it!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I grabbed the Thermalright Frozen Infinity 360 BLACK to replace my old weak 120mm Coolermaster fan from the previous build—it just wasn't cutting it anymore with the heat. My current setup is solid: latest Intel Core i7 (LGA 1851 socket on the MSI Z890 Gaming Plus Wi-Fi board), 48GB Corsair Dominator RAM and a beefy Corsair RMe1000x PSU to keep everything powered reliably on XMP_2.
This 360mm AIO is a huge step up. The blacked-out infinity mirror pump head looks clean and understated in my case—just subtle ARGB that matches the build. The three TL-M12 fans (2000 RPM max) push serious air (around 69 CFM) through the radiator, and it's kept my Core i7 temps in the low-mid 60s during heavy loads/gaming here in humid Lakeland, Florida. Idle stays chill in the 40s-50s, and it's quiet most of the time—pump doesn't whine, fans only get audible on full blast but PWM tuning keeps them tame.
Install was straightforward: full compatibility with Intel LGA 1851, mounting hardware included, flexible tubes, and it fit nicely on the MSI Z890 board without clearance issues (even with the tall Dominator RAM). No leaks, solid build quality for the price—Thermalright nailed the budget high-performer vibe again.
Only small complaints: Fans can ramp up noticeably under max stress if you're noise-sensitive, and the infinity mirror is cool but subtle (not as "wow" as some LCD ones). But for cooling performance vs. cost? It crushes my old air setup.
4.5 stars—perfect upgrade for this Intel rig. Temps dropped big time, and it's reliable for daily driving. Highly recommend if you're ditching weak cooling!

This is my 2nd time using this cooler for a build. Using the included thermal paste, my 12700kf sits at 27 idle and 52 MAX under load. The first build is going on 3 months with no issues at all. This is a newer cooler so we’ll see how longevity goes, but for now I have nothing to complain about.

Would highly recommend. Here’s a few things to note.

1. I built in an o11 vision. Extremely big case. The Thermalright tubes are actually smaller than most and stiffer. Because of this, the AIO actually wasn’t able to be mounted the correct way and is upside down. However, they include a black cover that blocks the logo so you don’t need to fully worry about the orientation.

2. The fans aren’t great. Extremely loud and when turned done have a small tone. However, they get the job done. I’m running them on the back of the radiator just for more airflow.

The RGB is alright, but note these are fans that cost $13 for 3, so don’t expect anything crazy.

3. The power cable is LONG. Not long enough to loop back around the case, but you definitely need to think about how you’re going to manage that cable.

Other than those small things, would definitely recommend this cooler. I’ve had a few high end brand name AIOs fail on me in a shorter time than I’ve had these, but that makes sense considering the amount I build.

5/5.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I’ve done a great deal of research for CPU coolers strictly under 50mm for a few years and this is the best one I’ve ever seen. And Im talking about the Full Copper version specifically.

For context I’ve previously I’ve owned an Alpenfohn Black Ridge and while cooling was great and was a top performer for its time, its fan was too loud being too close to the heatsink and causing turbulence. Putting the fan on top of the Ridge heatsink would be much quieter but would just increase the total height to 62mm+ which is definitely not ideal for me. Not only that, the heatsink is too massive so cool air doesn’t even pass through all its fins when using a 92mm fan. And because it’s so big I dont even have access to M.2 drives and Ram. Anyway I had too many problems with this that I realize it’s not good enough to be one of the most effective coolers.

Now with the Thermalright AXP90 X47 Full Copper, it performs slightly better (making it the best performing 47mm cooler from all the tests I’ve seen despite it’s much smaller heatsink), is much quieter, easy to assemble, and is so much smaller. My cpu stays at around 70-80C at max load, no turbulence because of the fan on top of the heatsink rather than under, and I can easily get access to my M.2 drive and ram sticks. Also the horizontal heatsink fins allow for hot air to make its way to exhaust through the front and back of my vertical case with almost no obstruction, rather than the bottom and top. This may be one of the reason this cpu cooler is more effective than the much larger Black Ridge.

One thing I don’t like is the color of the fan it comes with, so I replaced it with a ID-COOLING TF-9215 ARGB Case Fan 15mm (which is about as quiet and effective as a Noctua NF-A9 if not better). Keep in mind, I’ve heard of reports that the original ugly fan may actually be the best fan for this specific heatsink design, but I haven’t tested this myself.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I don't usually write negative reviews, and I've liked thermalright products. I've used some of their tower air coolers and they've been fine. I might not anymore after this. But this thing is disappointing in so many ways.
1). Just performance. So I thought I would use it on 5900x 2U install.. LOL.. 3900x .. mm no.. 5600x3d, ok let's start there. Open lid 2u with a fan blowing over system. I would like to add I have a 2u 5950x with a Noctua NH-L9x65 with a 120mm vent above cpu fan and Artic 80mm fans exhausting. Runs full load 24/7 around 80 Cel.. hot but I can live with that given the cpu. So this guy 5600x3d open case started with HiveOS and fully loaded I was getting 85-90 .. I reinstalled heatsink which I'll get to later changing thermal compound and cranking down a little more on the four mounting points... got it to 80-85 load.. with LID OFF.. lid on with Artic 80mm exhaust fans, right back to 90. I said HiveOS gotta be off.. Installed windows, updated, HWinfo, XMRig on full load , HWinfo reads 84 with lid off, I'd say HiveOS was spot on.... performance.. even with a vented lid would be terrible on anything but the weakest of processors. So for most, it doesn't work if you can't even handle a 5600x3d under load with a floor fan blowing on your, it should not be running warmer than a 5950x sitting in a rack.

2) Installation. This is not the cooler for your first time build or less experience. Trust me.. As others have pointed out if you are gonna mount it, you should use the long screws with the stock AMD plate.. don't mess with that spider thingy it comes with. I got stuck in a situation where I was troubleshooting cpus as well.. and this was the heatsink/fan I was stuck with at that moment.. I unmounted and mounted over 5 times on different cpus.. as mentioned.. I got good at it.. Doesn't mean I think it was cool. Yes you must remove motherboard to mount this so most people aren't going to like that. First you need to remove your backplate and test that it lines up with the 4 downward mounting screws and slides on and off with no friction or restrictions. Install cpu.. place the 5 dots of thermal paste on cpu.. Take the fan off the heatsink and lay bare heatsink upside down prongs facing up. Get some sponge something to support lower motherboard. Turn motherboard over cpu facing down toward heatsink, carefully lower over the four holes until heatsink touches cpu. The paste will act like a double sided tape sorta. Put the back plate on hoping you adjusted mounting pegs good enough and slide it down. Now use the only cool part of this kit, the little finger nut driver to tighten nuts down pretty tight, until you can almost not feel the little rubber washers give anymore. There.. you did it!! Hope you didn't damage cpu, board, or something else. Like I said I managed to do it over 5 times and still using it right now. It won't stick around, once I find it's replacement probably another Noctua that's twice as much, but it works.

Other things. for 34 bucks that's not dirt cheap... still 34 bucks if it doesn't work. And I wouldn't put this on an icebox inside an actual enclosed case.. Instructions are not good enough really. I had to look at it a bit and the parts before I saw what was what and how it fit together while looking at said pictures in instructions. Anyways.. I highly don't recommend for any installation.. and being a low profile many will be looking to fit it into smaller cases with higher heat loads.. I heavily advise against that as well. Pic is 5600x3d cpu 100%, lid off, and floor fan on it. I know most aren't trying to run a cpu at 100% 24/7 but I still think there's a better product out there. Hey it looks cool though!

EDIT::: Want to edit this review since I left such a nasty one. It turns out it was not the cooler's fault. I was comparing results from a MSI and an ASUS. The MSI was overvolting really all processors so of course under load they were running hot. I put a Noctua NH-L9x65 on it and temps were the same if not hotter. So after tweaking bios, the cooler can work and I was a little quick to judge before looking at all the factors. After undervolting the cpu, temps are tenable, similar to the Noctua and half the price around 80-82 C under full load. So 4 stars maybe 5 if it were not such a pain to install. But it does work and it still looks cool.

text:
I got this for a NAS case where it only just fits with a 14700K which boosts well above the coolers rating of 155W to 253W.

The fact its pure copper seems to do an excellent job of allowing it to still turbo boost to the full 5.5Ghz for short periods, only thermal throttling if there is a prelonged load. Though worth noting, even a single core at 60W will thermal throttle, because Intel push those cores so hard on default settings, under-volting may help but not risking stability issues on my home server. Its actually less of a problem on multi-threaded loads as the power is dissipated over the whole chip.

This is exactly what I needed as I have some PHP scripts that generates thumbnails on-demand to save disk space, rather than keeping permanent copies. As its only 100 images per page, its able to finish all thumbnails before saturating the coppers heat load, and being copper it dissipates that heat in seconds so the next page load still goes full power again.

So while it may not get full performance out of the CPU in all scenarios (again, its not designed for such a beastly CPU), it really punches above its weight for my use-case. I'm actually curious if replacing the fan with something of higher airflow might prevent the throttling entirely.

NOTE: I did use the Thermalright 1700 socket contact frame too, just to try to get the best thermal transfer. But this cooler clamps down quite tightly with 4 screws from under the motherboard so it may not have been necessary.

*STOP* are you sure your case can fit a 360mm AIO in your case? You checked? Okay good. Keep reading.

This review is written with the understanding that this product is far cheaper than the competition. I used some left over parts to upgrade my wife's casual gaming PC / our media room PC.

After 5 years it was finally time to upgrade my computer. While researching 360 AIOs, Thermalright kept coming up in my research. I have used their air coolers before and they were always solid, so I decided to give them a chance. I am beyond thrilled with the performance and quality of this AIO and can't recommend it enough.

- The mesh tubes are a little longer than other AIOs I reviewed, which I appreciated. Is great for the case I used (JONSBO 2-Chamber TK-3). Looks great and even has 3 "combs" on the tubes to help with looks.
- The included fans (ARGB) look great and move a lot of air while being much quieter than my previous AIO's fans (Fractal Prism 240) despite there being 1 more.
- The included magnetic screen looks GREAT and I am kind of amazed at the selection of included backgrounds and readout options. Reports by other reviewers of the software being bad I think may be outdated, because the software worked flawlessly for me and was able to do everything I needed it to, including adding custom logos and videos, layouts, etc. Really kind of amazing how good it is for the price.

I am over the moon about how good of a purchase this was. I think you can't really go wrong unless you're just looking for a specific branded look and to spend way more money (such as buying the ASUS ROG branded AIO, for example). If you want to save money and some thermals, this is the way to go without sacrificing seemingly any performance or looks.

text:
There are really only two choices when it comes to an affordable setback cooler, the Royal Knight and the Fuma 3. When it comes to performance the Royal Knight wins hands down and performs to within a few degrees of the vaunted Peerless Assassin. There are caveats compared to the Fuma 3 though and they add up.

The most important is that the fans are simply quieter on the Scythe and actually perform better than the Thermalright fans when cooler swapped. In a basic stress test the fans from the Scythe kept a 105w tdp 9700x at 85C vs 88C. Beyond the results, the Scythe fans also sound better and are uniform while the fans on the Royal Knight are louder and mismatched. The 25mm doesn't have rubber corners but instead uses pads that probably allows the fan to rumble and resonate. The 15mm seems to be step up model that has the nicer rubber corners but seems to whine at higher speeds.

Royal Knight is a good overall cooler and the three star rating is based on the listed price. When on sale the cooler is very good with an easy four stars and the only thing holding it back from being excellent and five stars is the odd fan selection that Thermalright went with.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Thermalright has consistently demonstrated one of two things: Either they have such a competitive advantage that they can produce outstanding products at half the price of their competition, OR their competition has been gouging their customers for years now. Thermalright air coolers already have a great reputation as a good "bang for the buck" option. Now their liquid coolers will too.

This Frozen Notte (Italian maybe? It's a stupid name) is priced at about half, or maybe less, of its nearest competitor as far as I can tell. Cosmetically, it looks fantastic. The infinity mirror works great, and makes an amazing visual for your PC. The fans are decent looking, and the RGB lighting is nice, if perhaps a bit bright at times.

Maybe you don't care about visuals and just want performance? I think it delivers here too. I'm running mine as an exhaust fan, so the radiator is already getting all the case heat along with CPU heat. With my 7900x processor, the max I run is about 80degrees C while on Flight simulator, which is perfectly acceptable to me. I wish it was a bit better, but then I feel the heat coming out of the case and wow, it puts off a lot. The radiator is obviously working to dump so much heat out the top of the case.

Noise is a bit high at times, although I don't have much to compare it to. Other high-end air cooled PCs I use (typically with a HUGE Noctura air cooler) get louder when under load. I don't know how this compares to other water coolers, but it's never intrusive. The pump on this is silent, I can't even tell it's running over the other case fans in the system. Oh, and the pump is inline with the water tubes, which means you really can't mount this wrong. The pump will NEVER be the high point of they system they way they designed it. You just can't do it wrong.

This thing is a real bargain. There are probably better coolers out there that will drop CPU temps by a couple of degrees. And they cost 2x or 3x what this one costs. They certainly don't look any better visually (although an LCD screen on the water block would be cool). At this price, getting anything else is just throwing money away. Buy it now, before they figure out they could charge more for it.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Ordered the Grand Vision 240. This is a very great AIO unit but it is suffered by one very bad deal breaking issue. First of all, the quality looks great, the cooling performance is extremely satisfactory, decently quiet, large awesome display with plenty of good options to customize your display and I was loving it. Installation to my AM5 socket wasn't nearly as breazy as my Corsair H100i. with that one I didn't have to remove the stock MOBO cooler bracket as I had to with this one but it's not like you to have to change coolers much anyways. It wasn't too hard though but you will have to lay your PC on it's side as you will have to push hard for the screws to thread (do not try it upright, you will not get both screws to start threading as the H100i I had before it was easy to mount without laying the PC on its side, and yes this does come with thermal paste.

The main issue (and is also well documented online) is the TRCC software used for the display eats up a huge amount of your CPU usage and will cause stutters and terrible framerates if you game with your system. It has to do with the monitoring for all the info that displays on the screen it seems. Again there is a lot of online info and a couple Youtube videos addressing the issue which also effects me as well. Many on Reddit have mentioned they have complained to Thermalright support but the issue has not been addressed. One new update released has not fix the issue however some have unchecked the HDD monitoring and fixed the problem for some people, but not most people including me, YMMV. Check this well before buying as I believe this affects many LCD Thermalright models. Turn off the software and don't use the screen, everything runs just fine but turn it on, my games will stutter and lag very badly. Might they possibly fix this with another update? Maybe but I don't want to play the update fix lottery as many times people are left hanging with no fixes to many software issues even with reputable companies. I have an Asrock Nova X870E MOBO, AMD 9700x, 32GB GSkill 6000 ram and a 9070xt and I feel like I can barely run solitaire with the display on.

Gamers are usually the target for AIOs to keep their systems cool so they shouldn't be having a product that is unoptimized for those people. I don't believe ALL people are effected so again YMMV and you might be fine, the cooling is great however and at worst if you don't mind turning off the screen while gaming, waiting for an update, or you don't use your system for gaming, by all means GO FOR IT!! Its great and for the price it would be unbeatable!! I just don't want to keep disabling the software, it kinda defeats the purpose of having an LCD display. I will be returning it for that reason and I'm not sure yet but I might get the Lian Li Galahad II though it's a bit more $$, but i will look in to any possible drawbacks first.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Used to cool a 9800X3D in a King 95 Pro case. Other components are 5070 ti, 32gb G Skill RAM, X870 mobo, 1 tb and 2 tb NVMe, 1200w PSU. Playing at 4K resolution.

I was skeptical about how this AIO would perform. There were few reviews on Amazon and almost nothing on other platforms. So far I've played a few demanding games and rarely does the CPU go above 50º C except for high CPU usage scenarios where it can reach 70º C. I am completely content with those numbers. For less than $70 (what I paid for it), what more could I ask for in terms of performance. Another plus is the noise level. I cannot hear the pump at all while at 100% speed.

The build quality is adequate. Nothing seems flimsy or poorly constructed. I'd say it's above average for the price. I cannot comment on the included fans since I swapped them to match my other fans (Montech AX and RX fans). I will say that they feel very rugged and durable, much better than the ones I swapped them for. I'd imagine they'd perform better than the Montech fans.

There are some cons, though. First, the instructions don't help very much. If you are versed in PC building, you won't have a problem but for a newbie, I can see it being an issue. Luckily, there are many resources online as to how to mount AIOs. Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be a tutorial for this specific unit. However, there are tutorials for other Thermalright AIOs and the method is the same. Something to keep in mind if you get confused, the mounting brackets for AM4 and AM5 are the same even though it only says AM4 on the brackets.

As for the LCD functionality, I have not done much within the app other than browse. It seems very basic and UI is unattractive and somewhat unintuitive. There are guides online on how to install the app and how to use it. I'd recommend looking those up because you might not be able to figure out how to load your own images and such. I will be tinkering with the app more in the future. I wanted to test the performance first.

In conclusion, this is a very good AIO at a very good price. The price had me skeptical, but I was confident that Thermalright wouldn't let me down. They have made a name for themselves in the PC cooling market and for good reason. I probably would not have purchased an LCD AIO at this price from another brand. That would be suspicious. Thermalright is known for producing quality products at some of the lowest prices in the industry. So if you're looking for a unit with an LCD screen, you can be assured this will fit the bill.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Full disclosure, I already own a Noctua NH-D15. I recently built a new rig with an Intel Core i5-13600K which is overclocked and runs pretty hot. I wanted to try something new versus my Noctua, which is a few years old now. Being a longtime fan of Thermalright since the AMD Athlon XP days, I bought the Frost Commander. The quality of the mounting hardware, heatsink, and fans are right up there with Noctua honestly. The whole thing has such a nice premium feel to it and it's just a fraction of the price. It even includes LGA1700 mounting hardware, something that DeepCool still doesn't do with the Assassin III.

Cooling performance is awesome too. On my 13600k which is running @ 1.36v, the Frost Commander keeps it cool enough to not thermal throttle, which is pretty crazy for an air cooler. I did compare it on my CPU to my NH-D15 and I didn't see any meaningful difference, which is a good thing. The Frost Commander easily cools as good as the D15 which has long been considered the 'king' of air coolers.

If I have to nitpick and come up with a complaint, it would be the noise profile. At low RPMs the included fans are pretty much inaudible, but once around 900-1000 RPM, there is a bit of a drone/hum to them. This goes away at faster speeds all the way up to the maximum RPM which is mostly the sound of rushing air, but that mid-RPM hum is a little annoying to me in my Fractal Torrent case. I may experiment with other fans on this cooler just to see if I can get a little bit better of a noise profile across the whole RPM range. I would still highly recommend this cooler though. Incredible performance for a very reasonable cost.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Thermalright should redesign the mounting system for the AMD socket AM5 platform.

Since the stock backplate now retains the LGA bracket, and Thermalright is simply poking a screw through the existing holes and using a nut on the backside to retain the system, the cheap nut driver they include with the kit for installation of the nuts makes awful contact with the backplate. It's also easy to strip the nut driver.

It's difficult to adequately tighten the nuts, and you're going to remove metal from the backplate. You don't want those tiny bits of metal floating around inside your case or on your components.

For the price, the cooler works fine for my application. The only gripe I have is the mounting system. I have used the exact same mounting system on an AMD socket AM4 platform, but since you can remove the stock backplate and use the backplate that Thermalright provides, installation is much smoother in that case.

The fan is not the quietest, however the cooler is relatively small and cheap, so that is to be expected. Definitely quieter and more performant than the stock AMD Stealth cooler that comes with most of their lower cost CPU's.

This is adequate to cool my Ryzen 9600X. For better results, I replaced the fan with https://www.amazon.com/Noctua-NF-A12x25-G2-PWM-Premium-Quality/dp/B0FC636JBS/ . I also used https://www.amazon.com/ARCTIC-MX-6-Conductivity-Non-Conductive-Non-capacitive/dp/B09VDLH5M6/ , instead of the included paste.

If using on an Intel CPU, be advised to use a contact frame, like https://www.amazon.com/Thermalright-Generation-Retrofit-Anti-Bending-Black/dp/B0CXF16317/ .

A cooler like this can noticeably help your VRM and SSD temperatures. Just be aware that it's only good for dissipating about 125 W. If you use a CPU that boosts well above that, it will thermally-throttle almost immediately.

text:
Thermalright frozen edge 240mm is what I am using for my SFF Gaming Rig. It's been about a week now since I installed this AIO cooler from Thermalright. So far so good the AIO cooler keeps my cpu temps cool. I have brand new Ryzen 7 5700X3D CPU. For my gaming needs it does the job well. I play mostly older title games from Total War series and other RTS games and those type of games does require a capable CPU. Back to the cooler I like the inexpensive Thermalright Frozen Edge 240mm cooler.
Under Heavy Load:
During intense gaming temperatures can rise, reaching 75-80°C or potentially even higher. Depends on if it's running a stress test but for gaming it's typically around 75-80°C. I'm not running benchmarks or plan to do anything crazy for this SFF Gaming Rig. Mostly gaming, web browsing, and for my personal investment business running multiple Charts, Excel spreadsheets. It's nothing crazy for my gaming rig.
Idle Temperatures:
Under normal idle conditions, temperatures hover around the 30s or low 40s. It's a very quiet SFF build when I'm not gaming. You barely can tell if it's on.

The reason why I didn't put 5 star is because of the Thermalright Frozen Edge radiator fans that comes with the cooler. It's got a low buzzing/humm coming from the fans that I noticed during a gaming session. When it's running at idle from normal use like web browsing or looking at Charts/Excel spreadsheets the fan doesn't have that buzz/humm noise at normal temperatures. Whenever I am playing games or if I run the CPU hot on certain applications then the noise becomes pronounced but it's not annoying enough or even bad it's just there when the fan is running on a higher RPM. I checked the AIO cooler pump and checked the radiator for the noise but it's not coming from either of those places. The buzzing/humm noise is coming directly from the radiator fans. I'm not planning to switch the fans out just yet because it's mostly noticable when the CPU runs hot during gaming sessions. That's when the fans are running at a higher rpm and the bearing inside the fan are probably making that noise. As of now I'll deal with the low buzz/humm and I'll update the review if anything changes since it's only been about a week of usage.

Long story short: I got this cooler, and when I installed it. Idle temps were not going above 40C.
I ran cinebench on stock settings, it hit 5.3GHZ with 90C. (Didn’t even hit 5.15 previously)
Upon making the PBO -30, it hit 5.34 GHz with temps being at 87-88C at the max. No crash, performance drops or anything whatsoever.
Tested few games, didn’t cross 50C at any point. (I have attached snapshots of hardware info as-well)

All in all, the MSI cooler costed me more than a $100 whereas this beast costed me less than 50%, giving me extra performance. I truly recommend this cooler.

text:
I installed this cooler on a customer's prebuilt HP desktop that was equipped with the stock, aluminum cooler. Her CPU was an I5-10400 (socket 1200 - 65w - 6 cores - 12 threads). This cooler lowered her idle temperatures by 7 degrees (from 93 to 86). It lowered her peak temperatures (75% load) by 24 degrees (from 186 down to 162). It also tightened up the core differential temperatures. The stock cooler had a spread of 11 degrees, between the highest & lowest core (under load). This cooler brought the spread down to 5 degrees between the highest & lowest core (under load).

The HP computer used the same bracket for the CPU retention mechanism as well as the fan mount. Fortunately, I was able to mount this new cooler using the stock retention bracket.

If you have a fairly low-powered CPU with limited height restrictions & are looking for a step up from the stock cooler, I wouldn't hesitate to give this one a try.

The stock heatsink was cleaned, new thermal paste was applied & heat cycled several times before testing. The new cooler was heat-cycled the same before testing. The ambient air temperature was 78 degrees for all tests.

Highly recommended.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I'll be upfront, I bought this for the heck of it. I was using a tri-stack aircooler that many regarded as legendary. But after one of it's fans died, I decided to browse for a new cooler. Seeing many aircoolers lose LGA 2011 compatibility stung a bit, and seeing that the only options left were high in price stung even worse.

Then I stumbled upon this gem. At first, I thought it was some sort of scam, or a poorly made product. Seeing how, especially these days, many vendors such as Corsair would gladly sell you basically the same product for $150 or more. But for $48 at the time of writing... why not give it a shot?

I'm not unfamiliar with Thermalright, as I've used their air coolers previously and found them to be an impeccable value, albeit with unclear mounting instructions.

The box contains a cardboard placeholder and some foam, simple but effective. I took out all of the necessary paperwork and mounting parts, and began reading the manual.

It was decently laid out with a page for each socket, and the parts were labeled with letters, referenced in the manual. Not bad! Mounting my 2011-3 brackets was pretty straightforward.

After mounting, I hooked up the two fans with a PWM splitter, attached to the CPU fan header. I hooked my pump into a case fan PWM, which I set to run at max speed. I always put my pump to full speed to prevent any speed fluctuations, as the gears in most AIO pumps are very fragile to changes in torque.

It's overall build quality is impressive; braided hoses with well sealed metal ends. The fans are already screwed in, with their correct orientation, and the finish on the radiator feels smooth to the touch. Albeit the mounting brackets for LGA 2011 had some rough edges that could cut you if you weren't a seasoned system builder.

After that, I took my 8-core xeon, and gave it a thorough stress test in Aida64 (CPU/FPU/RAM/Cache). My 1660v3 was at 4.3ghz, and 1.220v at the time of the first test. After 1 hour, it *peaked* at 61 degrees. I was worried none of my threads were being utilized, but the cores all had load, and the idle temps were around 22-23 before starting.

Unreal. For this price? What are you giving up?

Simple. It's not RGB. It does have an ARGB header for the screen on the pump to do temp readouts, but I couldn't be bothered. My board is too old to have that anyhow. Alongside the fans being rather noisy even at low speeds, but they push an insane amount of air for being cheaper included fans.

But... considering the performance at a fairly heavy overclock, what happens when you punish it severely?

I chugged my pot of coffee, still scalding hot, and managed to put my chip at an eyebrow-scorching 1.455v. Pinned it to 4.5ghz, opened Aida64, and let it rip.

Max core temp? 87 degrees. Package hit 89.

After one hour, at 1.455v, at literally 125% of it's base clock. On a platform known for making power bills turn into a medical bill.

If you paired this with a good set of quieter, high-RPM fans in push-pull, I'd see no issue with this cooling chips that draw 200+ watts under load effectively.

To say I am beyond impressed is an understatement. I am awestruck. I've used other cheap AIO's, but this unit is something else.

Do not let the price scare you. It is not a scam, and in fact, it'll gladly leave you another $100 in your budget for that higher-tier GPU.

Buy it.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I decided to try out a full compliment of Thermalright products in a "new" full rebuild of my system after having spent the past year or so using the Thermalright Peerless assassin tower cooler (hailed as one of the greatest air coolers ever, often very close to the performance of the king NHD15) with great results. I am very impressed with the value proposition from Thermalright products. They are extremely affordable and extremely effective, especially when considering the cost.

These fans and the 360AIO I put in my system on this rebuild are happily operating my system in a Cinebench R23 run with a 5 degree drop in CPU temp and overall multi-threaded score of 34326 at stock CPU settings with the exact same fan and radiator size configuration and BIOS settings. Literally all I did was take all the old stuff out, drop in the new stuff and power it on. I did not change settings in BIOS or fan curves whatsoever. For reference, this setup replaced a full Corsair kit, complete with Corsair 360AIO. Hands down this system is beating the brakes off of the Corsair setup, with less plugs and wires, no software needed, and simple plug and play operation, at a fraction of the cost. I bought the Thermalright equipment for the entire build for less than the cost of JUST the Corsair AIO, which I will be returning.

I have watched numerous product reviews on Thermalright components and the number one concern brought up is always longevity and warranty support, although nobody seems to have had to post a video about any of these AIOs giving up on them yet that I have seen. Since my last Thermalright cooler was an air-cooled tower, I cannot make a fair comparison here, but I can offer that even if this AIO dies, I can replace it 4-5 times and still come in at a lower cost than the Corsair AIO. I truly hope that I don't need to do that, but even if I did, it would be cheaper, still plug and play, and still no software issues or bugs, which warms my little heart.

Fan noise is a very subjective thing here in my opinion. I am running them at full speed during benchmarks for maximum cooling and yes you can hear them, sure they are "loud," but not nearly as loud as the Cosairs were, and on top of it, the tone is much less annoying. When lowering the fan profile to a "silent" configuration for casual use and gaming, they are nearly inaudible in my house. I don't know what my noise floor is in my house, but we do have kids and dogs and a TV running all the time, and hard flooring, so it is probably noisier in my house than most other's homes. That said, even when these fans begin to ramp up, I still don't hear them over all of that. I only hear them when I max them out. They have not had to ramp up that high during normal use, so unless I do it manually, it is literally of zero concern to me and I think you will have a similar experience. I know big name reviewers with decibel meters and controlled environments for testing can speak in much more detail with evidence here on the topic, but frankly, that is not how most of us live, probably. Overall, I think noise will not be an issue for you. If you are coming from Corsair like I did, they are quieter in the same configuration. I know that much. The tone is better as well whenever they do begin to ramp.

The lighting is great. They can get painfully bright if you want to. I have mine dimmed down so I have a splash of color without going blind. They are decently diffused. I have seen better, but at much higher cost. Sadly, I have also seen WORSE at higher cost. Overall, lighting performance is great. They do not have rings or side lighting, which I know if very popular currently, but I personally don't care for that feature. Only the fan blade light up on these, and I like it a lot. The frame of the fan does a good enough job to reflect or highlight the light to provide a clean and crisp look.

Construction is sturdy and gives me no impression of weakness. Anti vibration pads are built into the frame and present on both sides which is very nice. The included screws are very minimalistic and won't stand out or make your build look like it was bolted together with garbage hardware. Very slim and sleek hardware here. The bite of the screws into the material is firm and positive, without being so tight that you need to use any force to seat them.

If you are on the fence about Thermalright, get off the fence and jump on board. Save yourself a TON of money, get stuff that works amazing, looks amazing, and doesn't lock you into a hot garbage software eco-system.

text:
I had previous experience with Thermalright fans with the TL-C12C-2 fans, and though I'd give these a chance since I wanted to tone tone down the amount of lighting in my computer.

They are surprisingly quiet for $15 fans, can't even hear it without putting my ear to my tower. Ironically quieter than the be quiet! fans I previously had in my tower.
The RGB is amazing, its not super bright which I prefer, but offers a really nice outline, it's pretty well diffused but has noticeable hotspots which is to be expected for fans this cheap.
Don't know exactly how much air they push, but they push enough through my case and AIO to keep both my CPU (11700K) and GPU (7800XT) below 70 degrees celsius and still remaining whisper-quiet under full load.
Daisy=chaining them is definitely the cheapest that they were able to do, basic cable extensions that route off the PWM and ARGB cables, which isn't the greatest but they're so cheap that it's a wonder they can even daisy-chain in the first place.
Now, I bought 4 packs of these total, 2 packs of the standard model, and 2 packs of the reverse blade model. I was a little skeptical since other reviews had stated broken blades, but all of mine shipped with no damage whatsoever. QC might be a bit sketchy since they're so cheap and it also really depends on the shipping you get and whether or not you get an angry FedEX driver.
Price is unbeatable, each fan is $5 in this pack, or about $7-$10 if bought in singular packs, and are absolutely amazing value.

Yeah, I recommend these. Not the best fans in the world obviously, but they're so incredibly cheap that they're well worth the price. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Thermal paste quality needs two consideration: how well it dissipates heat and how long it’ll last until it experiences pump out.

If you can get the best of both worlds, you’ve found the absolute best thermal paste. The tfx doesn’t dissipate heat as well as my Noctua NT-H2 or the MX5. Expect the thermals to be 1-3c lower based on workload.

Where does this paste shines? Durability!!! It’s a rather thick paste to work with so best technique is to warm it up by putting it inside a ziplock bag, zip it up and submerge it into hot water for 5-10min to soften it up. It’s still pretty thick but MUCH easier to work with.

Since I installed it on my cpu and gpu, I’ve got no issues with them working for 1 week and the performance drops like I did with thinner pastes. I don’t need to worry about it oozing out between the two contact surfaces (pump out).

Do I recommend this paste? Depends!!!

If you want the absolute best in thermal conductivity, look at Liquid Metal. If you want easy to apply, this isn’t it. If you want to set it and forget it for over a year, this is the paste to go.

Dateline: A Tiny PC Case, a Space Where Every Millimeter is a Battlefield, 4:07 AM. There is a special kind of madness that drives a man to build a computer inside a box the size of a shoebox. It is a high-stakes game of inches, a brutal, three-dimensional chess match against the unyielding laws of physics. Your greatest enemy in this tiny, hot-box world is heat, and your greatest challenge is finding a fan that can fight it without demanding a space you simply do not have.

Standard 25mm fans are bloated, arrogant things in this domain. They are clumsy bulls in a china shop of miniaturized components. You need something specialized. Something lean, mean, and built for the trenches. You need the Thermalright TL-C12015B Slim Fan.

This is not just a fan; it is a miracle of engineering. A scant 15 millimeters thick, it is a wafer-thin sliver of high-performance potential. When you hold it, you expect it to be flimsy, a fragile piece of plastic compromise. But it is not. It feels solid, premium, a dense and well-built tool that belies its skeletal profile.

But the real shock comes when you power it on. For something this thin, you expect a polite, anemic puff of air. What you get is a hurricane. This slim blade moves a shocking, almost unbelievable amount of air. It’s a testament to some kind of aerodynamic black magic, a full-sized fan’s performance packed into a low-profile chassis. It’s the quiet, powerful engine that makes the impossible, high-performance ITX build a reality.

In the cramped, claustrophobic guts of a small form factor case, where a heatsink is fighting for space with a RAM stick and a cable is threatening to choke the life out of your airflow, this fan is your secret weapon. It fits where others cannot. It brings a rush of cool, life-giving air to components that would otherwise be gasping for breath, thermally throttling themselves into a state of pathetic submission.

And the value… the value is the final, beautiful punchline. In the boutique world of SFF building, where specialized parts often carry an absurd, "enthusiast" price tag, the Thermalright slim fan is a breath of fresh, affordable air. It delivers top-tier performance and solid build quality for a price that feels like a gift.

This is not just a good fan; it is an essential piece of kit for anyone brave or foolish enough to venture into the world of ITX builds. It is the problem solver, the space saver, the silent, powerful engine that keeps your tiny, beautiful creation from melting itself into a puddle of expensive slag. A highly recommended, five-star champion for the small-box warrior.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
TL;DR:
Pros:
1. Quiet even at the highest RPMs
2. Premium quality with no wobble
3. Compatible with iCUE and presumably other fan hubs/RGB controllers/RGB software suites
4. Bright LEDs with excellent color accuracy
5. 1PWM cable, 2 Male ARGB cables, 1 Female ARGB cable

Cons:
1. Distracting front logo that can be covered; becomes less bothersome at higher RPMs
2. LED diffusion isn't perfect regardless of selected color/effect but not a dealbreaker

Full Review:
A thorough review since this fan doesn't have any yet.

For backstory, I bought a prebuilt ASUS G16CH a few months ago and it had a severe lack of RGB with the exception of the LED strips towards the front of the case. So I started the project of slowly swapping out the stock hardware inside the case not including the GPU and CPU. I settled on Corsair as my ecosystem and got to work. I replaced the stock top exhaust fan with a 240mm Elite Capellix AIO/Radiator, added a front intake fan to match the radiator fans (all AF120 RGB), replaced the stock RAM, and added two sets of LC100 tiles.

The only thing that was left for me to swap out was plain black rear exhaust fan. Turns out the fan size was smaller than the standard 120mm or 140mm fan. After doing some research I discovered that most companies haven't bothered making 92mm RGB fans because they're not a common fan size, and finding one would be nearly impossible. On top of that, my motherboard has no RGB/ARGB headers so whatever fan I did find I would need to also work with my Corsair Commander Core.

From what I can tell at the time I'm writing this review, there are only about 4 92mm RGB fans on Amazon, two of which are 4-pin RGB fans, not 3-pin ARGB fans. There are no 4-pin RGB to 3-pin Corsair LED hub adapter cables, so that would cut my options in half.

And so I landed on this one. I'm not too familiar with Thermalright and I saw that this particular fan was relatively new, cheap, and had no reviews, so I decided to take a chance.

I was more than pleasantly surprised. It's built solid, the fan blades and housing feel premium. It comes with 4 case fan screws. There is 1 PWM cable to connect to a compatible motherboard or fan hub (in my case, the Commander Core, which I can use to change the RPM), 2 male ARGB cables and 1 female ARGB cable (I used a 3-pin ARGB adapter to make it compatible with a Corsair Lighting Node Pro).

This fan is quiet at the highest RPMs (running mine at 2,000 RPM), it doesn't wobble, and the LED lights inside are bright, pretty much on par with the Corsair fans in my case (AF120 RGB). While I'm not sure how many LEDs are in this fan, I added it as an 8-LED Series Fan in Corsair iCUE and all the effects work. The color accuracy when selecting colors in iCUE is perfect.

All that said, this fan does have a few small downsides. The first being that the diffusion of the LEDs inside isn't great, which means you'll see the location of each LED, regardless of what color they are. It could also just be the fan I received and someone else might have better luck. For me personally it's not a dealbreaker and it's not too distracting so I'm satisfied. The second downside is that the logo on the front is a bit distracting especially at lower RPMs because it gives the effect that the fan is wobbling when it isn't, but this can be fixed by either covering it with a sticker or turning up the RPM which is what I did.

Overall this satisfied my need for a 92mm RGB fan and considering the price it's a steal. This is a good start and I hope that we begin seeing more of them on the market as PC builds continue to become more compact.

Pros:
1. Quiet even at the highest RPMs
2. Premium quality with no wobble
3. Compatible with iCUE and presumably other fan hubs/RGB controllers/RGB software suites
4. Bright LEDs with excellent color accuracy
5. 1PWM cable, 2 Male ARGB cables, 1 Female ARGB cable

Cons:
1. Distracting front logo that can be covered; becomes less bothersome at higher RPMs
2. LED diffusion isn't perfect regardless of selected color/effect but not a dealbreaker

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text: Thermalright TFX is my top pick for thermal paste on GPUs and glass substrates, by far. Some find its thick texture hard to spread, but I don’t see this as a problem. After decades of experience, my current technique is to simply apply a central blob in the general shape of the surface, let the heatsink’s pressure spread it, and get great results, usually better than careful spreading (check YouTube videos for proof). The thick paste stays in place during GPU temperature swings, preventing pump-out better than most pastes. So far, it's lasted at least a few years in my tests with no degradation, so at worst the longevity is no worse than OEM pastes. It has low thermal resistance and high conductivity, isn’t electrically conductive (unlike liquid metal), and its easy to use. The main drawback is the price: 2g is costly and only covers about six GPUs if you’re careful. I recommend it for GPU refurbishing, but I wish Thermalright offered larger, cheaper quantities for non-OEM customers like me.

I have an AORUS GeForce RTX 3080 XTREME WATERFORCE 12G and I thought it was getting too hot this Summer. There was nothing wrong but I felt like I could improve it.

Max temps of 61-62C at 85F ambient. (my PC is in a garage in Ventura CA with no air conditioning as of 17AUG23 2PM - day of my testing) My GPU clock is set at +130 which can be a clock speed of 2040 to 2200 stable and draws around 350-360W of power. I can't increase power sadly because its 2x8Pin instead of 3x8Pin(come on Gigabyte!)

I took my GPU apart which was super easy on an AIO cooled GPU. 10 total screws later it was open. I used the advise of every other review to heat the paste in hot water before application.
I placed it in hot to the touch but not boiling water for a couple minutes inside a ziploc bag but it was still a little tough to spread. It takes a little longer than other thinner pastes, but spreads eventually. Once I was satisfied with the coverage I put it all back together and tested it in benchmarks and longer looping tests.

I was able to drop my temps down to 57-58C in the same 85F ambient temp(I used a digital ambient temp thermometer to make sure it was at the same temp as it was before.)

Hot spot went from 72C to 67-68C.
Temps are even better at night but I wanted to test it at the hottest time of the day to see how it held up.

Overall my boost clocks are a bit higher now and my OCD is happy to see temps below 60C!
I also have a Thermalright CPU AIO and 12/13th Gen CPU Frame from them as well and they make some banger budget products.

Highly recommend!

text: I am genuinely stunned by the performance of this thermal paste in my gaming laptop. For reference, I've got a Legion 5i that is equipped with an i9 149000hx, which is essentially a desktop CPU crammed into the confines of a laptop chassis. Other pastes are too thin, and once the fans go back on, and the temperatures go up, it just oozes out. So, yeah. If you're gaming on a laptop, and you're dealing with stupidly high temperatures, I highly recommend this paste. Don't do the dot method or the line method, though. Use the spreader, and make sure there is full, even coverage.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this Thermalright ARGB controller for a fairly niche use case. I had already ordered a Nollie (a different, more expensive ARGB controller with more features), but it won't arrive for multiple weeks and I wanted to test my new ARGB fans before their return window closes.

This controller is cheaper and has fewer features than the Nollie, but all I planned on using it for was to hook up all of my new fans to it on a table to make sure their LEDs work properly (good brightness, even lighting, good quality colors).

It's surprisingly well built for its price and it did everything I needed it to with my fans' ARGB. It has a nice selection of colors and lighting modes available, although I would've liked to see a fine-tuning option for the colors - up and down arrow buttons to incrementally increase or decrease the amount of red, green, and blue light in the mix to get exactly the color you want. If it had that feature, I'd also like a way to save a few specifically tuned colors to profile buttons as well. But this is a roughly $12 controller, so those may be a unrealistic requests.

The remote has all of the buttons I would want for this controller and it worked perfectly; however, I had the controller on a table right next to the remote, not installed in a PC case, so I can't confirm how well it would work through a metal case panel.

I did not test the Thermalright controller's PWM passthrough feature as I already had a separate fan controller set up. But based on how well its ARGB features worked, I have no reason to doubt its PWM capabilities.

I'm generally wary of buying cheap electronics from no-name brands and plugging them directly into my expensive devices. However, unlike those no-name "brands" that sell relabeled questionably-designed products, Thermalright is a known brand that has built a good reputation for itself at this point. Of course, even reputable brands have produced bad quality products, but after trying this controller I have no concerns about using it.

If I didn't want something with more advanced levels of control, I would have no problem using this in my PC. Since I've already ordered a Nollie though, I'll keep the Thermalright around as a bench tester for any new ARGB devices I buy in the future.

If you're looking for a way to light up your fans without dealing with the mess that is most ARGB control software, I think you'd have a hard time finding a better option than this from a known brand for roughly $12.

(In case this product page is modified in the future, this is a review of the "Thermalright ARGB and Fan HUB X12 IR Black Hub Controller".)

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I am one of those people who has a passion for quieting annoyingly noisy PC fans. Some fan noise is more annoying than others. The mere sound of spinning flan blades usually isn't as terrible as bearing noise. Noctua is my "go to" fan because they simply are the best.. no bearing noise. There isn't anything as consistently quiet as Noctua. However, I was working in a compact PC this time and designing a custom CPU cooler. Space was limited and Noctua doesn't make an 80mm x 15mm fan so I needed another option. I have used Thermalright fans before when I designed a custom cooler for one of my graphics cards and it worked well. Thermalright is the quietest alternative to Noctua that I have found. The fact that it is 2/3 the price is a bonus.

I tested an 80mm x 25mm Noctua against this 80mm x 15mm Thermalright and they sounded the same to me. Granted, the specs on these 2 are not identical and my test was not using a db meter, but when I work on computers day in / day out, I am using my ears, not a db meter, so that's what matters.

This fan is so quiet that I will have to rethink whether or not I need to ALWAYS spend the extra money on Noctua. It will take a couple years to answer that question fully. Noctua fans seem to stay quiet for years. I just don't have that much data on the Thermalright.

text: This thing definitely improves upon the standard retention bracket. Dropped my temperatures by a few Celsius just by itself. I wasn't sure about all the hype, but I'm a firm believer now. The 14th gen i9 chips get so hot that any improvement in temps is more than welcome. Plus, the additional benefit of keeping that CPU from bending or warping over time, as this bracket clamps down evenly around the chip. I decided to opt for a Noctua NH-D15 dual-tower, dual-fan setup on top of this thermalright plate and I've got temps to manageable levels without much concern that I'm topping out my temps and throttling the cpu. The included thermal paste is a bonus. It spreads well and performs well. I ordered my go-to Arctic MX-4 intending to use it, but the thermalright paste is proving to be very efficient. I'll be using these mods for all future builds. Beware, just do not tighten with too much force. I use 2 fingers on the included hex key / allen wrench and apply just enough force to secure the plate to the board, then I back it off by 1/8th of a turn. Plenty of YouTube vids covering the installation and performance of these brackets, so go ahead and get familiarized with the product before purchase and installation. This gets my highest 5/5 star recommendation.

UPDATE:
There are two things I find objectionable about this PC. First is the inadequacy of the user documentation. The online user manual provided is a generic "get acquainted with your pc" document with no specific details on the particular model itself. There is no guidance available on how to upgrade any of the internal components, nor any mention of the existence of such documentation. Fortunately there are a few YouTube videos of the processes available to give enough information to do what I intended to do.
Second, the case itself has provisions for two additional 2.5" SATA drives but only one additional power cable connection is provided which connects to one of two 6-pin power sockets on the motherboard. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
TL;DR: The Acer Nitro is a solid budget-friendly gaming laptop that balanced school and gaming well. Loud fans, weak battery gaming, and fragile screen were drawbacks, but it handled demanding games at high settings and was great for a student lifestyle who fancies gaming in free time.

I used my Acer Nitro V 15 daily for both school and gaming, and for the price, it really impressed me with how versatile it was. Definitely felt like a purchase worth it.

As a full time college student taking online classes, this laptop was more than enough for productivity. Typing was seamless for the many essays and assignments I had to crank out, and it handled regular browsing with multiple tabs without breaking a sweat. I don’t do heavy creative work like video editing, but for what I did use it for, it never let me down.

Gaming was where it really surprised me. Titles like Red Dead Redemption 2 and The Last of Us Part II ran great at high settings, delivering smooth, immersive gameplay that felt way beyond what I expected at this price point. Paired with an external 2K 144Hz monitor at times and it kept up without any issues.

Portability was another big win. While it isn’t the lightest laptop out there, carrying it in a case made it easy to take from work to the library or just toss in my backpack. Honestly, I barely noticed the weight after a while.

Of course, there are trade-offs. The fan noise is one to note. On auto, it can get loud under load, and on max, it’ll easily fill a quiet room. That said, cooling does its job, and with headphones it wasn’t a dealbreaker. The other thing: gaming unplugged was basically a no-go. Performance dropped heavily on battery, which surprised me at first, but since I always had access to an outlet, it didn’t really affect my routine. On light use like schoolwork or browsing, I’d get about 2–3 hours on battery.

The display itself was fine, standard but enjoyable. Unfortunately, mine cracked after about a year from what felt like light pressure, which was disappointing and ultimately why I’m moving on to a new laptop.

On the bright side, upgrading was a breeze. I swapped in 32GB of RAM and added a 2TB SSD, which gave me more headroom for multitasking and plenty of storage for my game library. That definitely added to the experience.

Overall: The Acer Nitro V 15 delivered a great balance of school and gaming performance in a portable package. It’s not flawless, the fans get loud, battery gaming is basically impossible, and the screen durability left me wanting more, but for the time I used it, it played the games I wanted at high settings and fit perfectly into my student lifestyle. For the price, it’s a solid entry into gaming laptops.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Let me start with this first, I like this laptop and I think it's a very good buy.

The best thing about this laptop is the big 17.3" IPS screen, it's sharp with good viewing angles and decent brightness.

The 11'th gen Intel CPU performs very well, everything loads very fast and it handles multiple tasks with ease.

Wireless connectivity is also great, connection is fast and stable.

The speakers are decent for a laptop, OK, nothing more.

The keyboard is good and spacious but I wish that the keys were bigger, there's a lot of space in this laptop to fit larger keys like CTRL, ALT etc. and especially the small up/down arrow keys are requires more attention because I find myself hitting the shift key when trying to press the UP arrow key or the UP key while wanting to press the DOWN key.

I am also missing a light indicator for the Caps&Num lock keys.

The touch pad is large and comfortable to use, responds very well.

Battery life seems decent, I haven't tested it too much but it seems you can squeeze out at least 4-5 hours of work maybe more if you use lower brightness.

Regrading ports, you get 2xUSB3, 1xUSB-C (5gbps), 1xHDMI (2.0), 1xRJ45 LAN, 1xUSB2, 1x3.5mm audio - good but I wish Acer had included Thunderbolt 4 since the 11'th gen Intel processors support it.

One point I would like to raise is the lack of (any) technical information regarding this laptop, no detailed specs regarding RAM, NVMe SSD drive besides the size, no technical info, upgrade parts, IPS panel color gamut specs etc.

I wanted to upgrade the RAM and I could not find any info which RAM this laptop has and what speed it's running.
So for other potential buyers I want to share what I have found:

This laptop comes equipped with 8GB DDR4-2666MHZ dual channel memory (4GB soldered on board + 1X4GB expansion module).
This seems a bit odd to me because according to Intel specs the 11'th gen I5 and I7 supports DDR4-3200MHZ, so I can't figure out why Acer used lower speed memory ?
Who knows, not a deal breaker but little bit disappointing and I wish that this info was written somewhere for potential buyers.

The 1 memory module you can upgrade is a Kingston 4GB DDR4-2666MHZ model: ACR26D4S9S1KA-4 .

I wanted to upgrade the RAM to 20GB by replacing it with a 16GB module and I also wanted to preserve some of the dual channel functionality by utilizing Intel's dual channel "flex mode" because the memory modules do not mach in size.
So I have bought the most similar spec'd 16GB DDR4-2666 module I could find locally made by Kingston model: KVR26S19S8/16.

Installed the module and the laptop booted with no problem, identified the new RAM properly and also enabled dual channel - great but again I wish someone had written what compatible memory you need to buy in order to upgrade.

The 512GB NVMe SSD installed is made by Kingston, you can also install an additional SSD for more storage.
Acer included a bracket mounted inside the laptop with a cable already connected and you also get a bag with 4 screws to mount the additional SSD drive.

So overall a very good laptop for daily work, web browsing and watching movies, fast CPU, I really like the large sharp screen and the big keyboard layout, price is great for what you get but I would prefer a faster RAM configuration and 2 RAM slots without on board RAM.

Acer could have perfected this laptop by doing some minor changes to the keyboard, putting a larger capacity battery and offering 16GB version for a bit more but I guess there are compromises you have to take when aiming for a competitive price point.

Hope this helps...
